spec.experiment_matrix_from_plan: Research plan (연구 계획 흐름): build NVMeVirt, survey configs, check whether the FTL mapping size can change (default 4K), then fio (libaio): (a) 4K-mapping SSD x randwrite bs {4k,8k,16k,32k,64k,128k} -> BW, clat; (b) 16K/32K-mapping SSD x the same bs -> BW, clat; record every numeric config. Report 1.1/4 recommends MAP {4 (baseline), 8, 16, 32 KB} on one fixed 970 Pro config (FLASH_PAGE 32 KB). User's run: MAP {4K,8K,16K,32K,64K,128K} x bs {4k,8k,16k,32k,64k,128k} x 3 reps = 6 x 6 x 3 = 108 runs of 60 s (~108 min of fio time plus per-run rmmod/insmod). Six module builds: MAP 4/8/16/32K use FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=KB(32), MAP 64K uses KB(64), MAP 128K uses KB(128); BLKS_PER_PLN=384 in all. Later phase (not this run): RocksDB db_bench / YCSB-A/B/F, WAL small IO and SST blocksize 4k vs 16k.
user_overrides_vs_report: Capacity: report recommends 64 GiB (memmap_size=64G, start chosen from /proc/iomem); user uses 12 GiB at 12G-24G (grub memmap=12G$12G, insmod memmap_start=12G memmap_size=12G). Storage = 12 GiB - 1 MiB, logical device ~11.21 GiB after OP 7%.
BLKS_PER_PLN: report 2048 (for 64 GiB -> 2 MiB block); user 384 (12 GiB / (384 x 16 dies) = 2 MiB). Same 2 MiB block intent; verified block = 2,097,152 B for every MAP.

NVMeVirt cores: report 5 (dispatcher 1 + workers 4); user 3 (cpus=3,4,5 -> dispatcher 3, workers 4,5). Report warns 1 worker bottlenecks at QD32/128 KB; 2 workers meets README minimum but may still cap large-bs throughput.
Host DRAM: report >= 128 GB; server has 24 GB (MemTotal ~11.45 GiB after reserving 12 GiB). Host: i5-13600K, 6 CPUs online (0-5, 1 thread/core), isolcpus=3-5.

Mapping set: report 4/8/16/32 KB with one NAND config (FLASH_PAGE 32 KB). User adds 64K and 128K with FLASH_PAGE_SIZE = MAP (ONESHOT = FLASH_PAGE x1), which changes NAND geometry for those two points.

Prefill: report measures after sequential prefill (steady state); user does no prefill, rmmod+insmod before every run, ramp_time=0, so the pre-GC (FOB) phase and the GC onset are both inside the 60 s window.
Repetitions: report does not fix a count; user 3 per cell.
numjobs: report 1 plus optional 4 check; user 1 only.

Report 1.3/4 suggests deciding (with the senior) whether to patch the other 4 KB assumptions (ssd.c:355, ssd.c:394, conv_ftl.c:867) and to add RMW latency; user's plan changes only ssd.c:73 and ssd_config.h, so these remain unpatched (must be stated in the record).
Optional sensitivity runs in the report (tPROG TLC 390 us, non-zero tBERS) are not part of the user's run.
Kbuild: user follows the report (CONFIG_NVMEVIRT_SSD); this overrides the upstream default (CONFIG_NVMEVIRT_NVM), not the report.
Kernel: report needs >= 5.15; server 6.8.0-142-generic (Ubuntu 24.04.4) is compliant, no override. fio version on server is 3.36 (report has no fio version recommendation).
caveats_from_report: No prior work changed the mapping unit: 0/15 surveyed papers, and all 5 public NVMeVirt forks keep secs_per_pg = 4096/LBA_SIZE, so there is no published baseline for this axis (report 1 / 1.3 / Appendix D).

ssd.c checks FLASH_PAGE_SIZE % pgsz == 0 and ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE % pgsz == 0: with a 32 KB flash page, 4/8/16/32 KB pass and 64 KB fails (report 1.3). This is why the user sets FLASH_PAGE_SIZE = MAP for 64K/128K.

Other hard-coded 4 KB assumptions: ssd.c:355 write-buffer latency counted per 4 KB; ssd.c:394 4 KB read latency applied only when xfer is exactly 4096 B; conv_ftl.c:867 4 KB firmware read latency for reads <= 4 KB (x nr_parts). They must be reviewed when the mapping unit grows (report 1.3). For randwrite-only runs the read paths matter only through GC reads (gc_read_page uses xfer_size = pgsz, so MAP=4K uses the 4KB read latency and MAP>=8K the full-page latency, a ~0.25 us difference).

conv_write() allocates a new page for every mapping unit touched and has no read-modify-write latency: a 4 KB write under a 16 KB map raises WAF but adds no read delay (report 1.3; implement RMW if needed).
Data is copied by LBA into the reserved memory (io.c); the FTL is only a timing model, so changing the mapping unit does not corrupt data (report 1.3).
maptbl (8 B/entry) and rmap (8 B/entry) are vmalloc'ed in host kernel memory outside the reserved region (report 1.3); for 12 GiB this is 48/24/12/6/3/1.5 MiB for 4K..128K.
The 970 Pro bundle has erase latency 0, so GC cost is underestimated unless tBERS is set (report 1.1, 4).
Multi-plane is not modeled in the base FTL (PLNS_PER_LUN 1; ssd.c 'TODO: to fix under multiplanes') (report 1.1).
With 1 I/O worker NVMeVirt becomes the bottleneck at QD32 / 128 KB; README minimum is 2 cores (report 1.1). User's 2 workers sits below the report's 4.

memmap start must be a free physical range taken from /proc/iomem and match grub; storage = memmap_size - 1 MiB (report 1.1/1.2). On this host /proc/iomem addresses are masked for non-root, so confirm with sudo that 12G-24G is inside System RAM.

Papers rarely report SSD config values (channels 6/15, OP 1/15, mapping unit and GC thresholds 0/15); the record should list both the changed values and the untouched defaults (report 2.3, 4, slide 14).
Before interpreting results, decide (with the senior) whether to fix the 4 KB assumptions and the missing RMW/erase modeling (report 4, slide 14).

Code-derived, not in report: for MAP 64K/128K, raising FLASH_PAGE_SIZE also raises ONESHOT (program unit) and GLOBAL_WB_SIZE (1 -> 2 -> 4 MiB) and doubles/quadruples per-die program bandwidth (32/64/128 KB per 185 us), so 64K/128K points are not same-NAND comparisons with 4-32K; document this as a confound.

Code-derived, not in report: write-buffer accounting is asymmetric. conv_write calls buffer_allocate(host IO size) but the NAND completion releases pgs_per_oneshotpg * pgsz (one flash page). When bs < MAP (e.g. MAP 16K bs 4K), more is released than allocated, the buffer's 'remaining' grows past its size, and write-buffer back-pressure disappears, so throughput in bs < MAP cells may be optimistic.

Code-derived, not in report: on a fresh device GC starts when free lines <= 2 of 384 per partition (~99.5% of 12 GiB physical consumed). At the measured ~250 MiB/s for MAP4K/bs4K, 60 s writes ~14.6 GiB, so GC should start around 48-50 s. Higher throughput or bs < MAP (each IO consumes a whole MAP page) moves the onset earlier, so per-second BW/latency logs are needed to separate the phases.
Previously measured MAP=4K/bs=4K/QD32 on this server: ~64K IOPS / 250 MiB/s (user-supplied; useful as a sanity check for the first run).

ctx.research_goal: 고용량 SSD에서는 4KB 매핑 기준 L2P 매핑 테이블이 용량의 약 0.1%에 해당하는 DRAM을 차지한다(1TB에 약 1GB, 256TB급이면 256GB). 이 부담을 줄이려고 FTL 매핑 단위를 키웠을 때 생기는 성능 비용을 정량화하는 것이 목표다. NVMeVirt(conventional FTL, page 크기 = 매핑 단위)의 매핑 단위를 4K/8K/16K/32K/64K/128K로 바꿔 가며 fio libaio randwrite(iodepth 32)로 대역폭(BW)과 완료 지연(clat)을 측정한다. 이를 통해 매핑 단위보다 작은 랜덤 쓰기가 겪는 RMW·쓰기 증폭 손실과 DRAM 절감(16K 기준 약 1/4) 사이의 트레이드오프를 보인다. 이 결과는 이후 RocksDB 튜닝의 근거로 쓴다. 대상은 16KB 미만 소형 I/O인 WAL과 SST block_size 4K→16K다. [확인 필요] '연구 계획 흐름' 메모는 매핑 단위마다 fio bs를 4K~128K로 스윕하도록 적혀 있다. 반면 사용자 요청에는 bs가 명시되어 있지 않으므로, 실험 매트릭스를 '매핑 6종 x bs 6종'으로 할지 사용자에게 확인해야 한다.

papers.title: FTL 매핑 단위에 따른 성능 분석 연구 (Google Gemini 대화 기록 PDF 출력본)
papers.venue_year: 학술 논문이 아님. gemini.google.com 대화 내보내기(2026-10-01 출력)이며 동료심사를 거치지 않은 자료
papers.relevance: SSD 고용량화로 매핑 테이블용 DRAM이 커지면서 매핑 단위가 4KB에서 16KB로 커지는 추세를 배경으로 깔고, 업로드된 세 논문(Power_analysis, SFTL, ZMS)을 요약한다. 핵심 가설은 '4KB 랜덤 쓰기를 16KB 매핑에서 처리하면 나머지 12KB를 읽어 합쳐 써야 하는 RMW가 생기고, 그 결과 쓰기 증폭(WA)·지연 증가·IOPS 하락이 필연적으로 따른다'는 것이다. 후반부는 RocksDB를 타겟 응용으로 정한다. WAL은 4KB 이하로 내려가고, SST는 block_size를 4K에서 16K로 튜닝할 수 있으며, 4K block에 16K 매핑이면 읽기 증폭이 생긴다고 정리한다. 이를 바탕으로 16KB 정렬 아이디어(지연 기반 그룹 커밋, 제로 패딩)를 제안한다. 주의할 점이 있다. DapuStor J5060(122TB, 4K/8K/16K 매핑, 16KB randwrite 30K IOPS)과 APSys'17 'TO FLUSH or NOT'은 Gemini가 외부 정보로 덧붙인 내용이라 검증되지 않았다. 또 'SFTL이 GC 비용과 fio IOPS 하락을 정량화했다', 'ZMS가 매핑 단위별 성능 트레이드오프를 분석했다'는 서술은 원문과 다르다. 따라서 논문에서는 원 논문을 직접 인용해야 한다.

papers.title: ZMS: Zone Abstraction for Mobile Flash Storage (Joo-Young Hwang et al., Samsung Electronics / KAIST)
papers.venue_year: USENIX ATC 2024 (2024 USENIX Annual Technical Conference, Santa Clara, July 10-12, 2024)
papers.relevance: Supplies the standard DRAM-cost motivation. With 4 KiB page mapping and 4-byte entries, the L2P table is about 0.1% of capacity (a 4 TiB SSD needs 4 GiB of DRAM). When the table does not fit, on-demand map caching causes misses: 27.1% of 4 KiB random reads over 8 GiB in the baseline UFS, and ZMS gives 37-44% better random reads. Its multi-granularity L2P (4 KiB page, 4 MiB chunk, zone) shows that coarser mapping saves a lot of memory: a chunk entry cuts map-cache memory by 1024x, and zone mapping is about 1/10^6 of page mapping. Writes smaller than the program unit (96 KiB TLC unit, 384 KiB superpage) cause an 'unaligned buffer flush', which doubles device writes. This is the analogue of sub-unit writes on a coarse mapping unit. The paper also says dummy padding is not recommended, because it wastes space and breaks write-pointer matching. ZMS reports 2.9-6.4x lower write amplification and 5.0-13.6x higher random-write performance. It targets mobile ZNS UFS with FIO 4 KiB random writes and is not a mapping-unit sweep, so it works as motivation and related work rather than as a direct baseline.

papers.title: Subpage-based Flash Translation Layer For Solid State Drivers [sic] (Mincheol Kang, Wonyoung Lee, Soontae Kim, KAIST)
papers.venue_year: Venue is not printed in the extracted text. References run up to 2015, so circa 2016; likely IEEE/ACM ICCAD 2016 (verify before citing)
papers.relevance: This is the most direct quantitative evidence on granularity. It uses page-level mapping, so the page size is the mapping unit, and sweeps 4/8/16/32 KB pages. As the unit grows, the share of subpage (sub-unit) writes grows: with a 64 MB write buffer it averages 26% at 8KB and 41% at 16KB (max 45% and 61%). These writes cause RMW (old data must be read before the write), longer write response time, internal fragmentation and program disturb. About 20% of RMWs are 'unnecessary' at every page size. The proposed size-aware LRU merging plus a page-state (sector bitmap) mapping table cuts NAND writes by up to 23% (13% on average). At 16KB the cut is up to 30% (19% on average), and at 32KB up to 36% (24% on average). It also brings subpage writes below 2% and cuts write response time by up to 14% (8% on average), at the cost of a larger mapping table. The study is trace-driven (NANDFlashSim with an OpenSSD-style FTL, MSR Cambridge traces), so it gives expected magnitudes but no fio BW or latency numbers.

papers.title: Power Consumption Characterization of Flash Memory SSD (Seungyong Shin, Dongkun Shin, Sungkyunkwan University)
papers.venue_year: Venue and year are not stated in the extracted text. Page numbers 14-18 and references up to 2009 suggest Korean conference or workshop proceedings, circa 2010
papers.relevance: Gives empirical evidence of a 16 KB address-mapping unit in commercial SSDs (SLC 64GB and MLC 30GB, NTFS, modified uFLIP). In the alignment test, random writes shifted by 0.5-8 KB cost more energy (J/MB) than aligned ones, while shifts that are multiples of 16 KB match the baseline. The explanation is that the SSD reads two 16 KB units, modifies them and writes them back (RMW). In the granularity sweep (1 KB-4 MB), random writes smaller than 16 KB have much higher J/MB while average power (W) stays flat or drops, because reads draw less power. At 16 KB and above, writes behave normally. Dirty, GC-active SSDs consume more energy than clean ones, which supports separating pre-GC and post-GC measurements (rand_time=0). The paper is also a method precedent: alignment and size sweeps can reveal a device's mapping unit.

papers.title: 연구 계획 흐름 (내부 연구 계획 메모)
papers.relevance: 본 연구의 동기와 실험 설계를 정의한 메모다. 배경은 다음과 같다. SSD의 FTL 맵(LPN→PPN)은 SRAM/DRAM에 있고, 매핑 단위는 512B → 4K → 16K(고용량 SSD)로 커져 왔다. 1TB SSD에는 DRAM 약 1GB가 필요하고, 4K 매핑을 유지하면 128/256TB급에는 약 256GB가 필요하다. 16K 매핑이면 이를 64GB로 줄일 수 있다. 수행 계획은 네 가지다. (1) NVMeVirt를 설치하고 다른 논문들이 쓰는 설정(총 용량 등)을 조사한다. (2) NVMeVirt에서 FTL 매핑 크기를 바꿀 수 있는지와 기본값을 확인한다. (3) fio(libaio)로 4K 매핑 SSD와 16K/32K 매핑 SSD 각각에서 randwrite 4K~128K를 돌려 throughput(BW)과 clat을 측정한다. (4) 설정값을 상세히 기록한다. 활용 응용은 RocksDB다. WAL은 16KB 미만 소형 I/O이고, SST는 block_size를 기본 4K에서 16K로 바꾸면 성능이 오를 것으로 예상한다. (메모에 있는 서버 접속 정보는 의도적으로 옮기지 않았다.)

expected_effects: DRAM 절감: 매핑 테이블 크기는 매핑 단위에 반비례한다. 4KiB 단위에 4B 엔트리를 쓰면 용량의 약 0.1%다(ZMS: 4TiB에 4GiB, 연구 계획: 1TB에 약 1GB). 16K 매핑이면 약 1/4로 줄어든다(연구 계획과 Gemini 기록 모두 256TB급에서 256GB를 64GB로 계산). 같은 비례를 적용하면 8K는 1/2, 32K는 1/8, 64K는 1/16, 128K는 1/32이다. 이 값들은 원문에 없는 도출값이다. 참고로 ZMS는 chunk(4MiB) 매핑으로 맵 캐시 메모리를 1024배, zone 매핑으로 약 1/10^6까지 줄인다. 반대로 맵이 메모리에 다 들어가지 않으면 map miss가 생긴다(ZMS 기준 랜덤 읽기의 27.1%).

RMW: 쓰기 크기가 매핑 단위보다 작거나 정렬되지 않으면, 해당 단위의 기존 데이터를 읽어 병합한 뒤 단위 전체를 다시 써야 한다. Power_analysis는 16KB로 정렬되지 않은 쓰기에서 16KB 단위 2개를 읽고 수정해 기록한다고 본다. Gemini 기록은 4KB를 쓰려면 나머지 12KB를 추가로 읽어야 한다고 설명한다. SFTL에 따르면 서브페이지 쓰기는 이전 데이터를 먼저 읽어야 해서 RMW를 늘리고, RMW의 약 20%는 새 데이터가 기존 데이터를 완전히 덮는 '불필요한 RMW'이다. 이 비율은 page 크기와 무관하다. 정렬되어 있고 크기가 매핑 단위 이상인 쓰기에는 RMW가 없다(Power_analysis: 16KB 배수 시프트는 기준과 같다).

WAF/쓰기량: SFTL은 매핑 단위(page)가 커질수록 서브페이지 쓰기 비율이 늘어난다고 보고한다. 8KB에서 평균 26%(최대 45%), 16KB에서 평균 41%(최대 61%)다. 병합만으로도 NAND 쓰기를 최대 23%(평균 13%) 줄일 수 있었다. 16KB에서는 최대 30%(평균 19%), 32KB에서는 최대 36%(평균 24%)다. 기본 FTL이 큰 단위에서 그만큼 쓰기를 낭비한다는 뜻이다. ZMS는 프로그래밍 단위 미만의 비정렬 플러시가 디바이스 쓰기를 2배로 만든다고 하며, 정렬 기법으로 E2E WAF를 2.9~6.4배 개선했다. Gemini 기록은 '4KB WAL 쓰기가 16KB 매핑에서 막대한 쓰기 증폭을 일으킨다'고 쓴다. 이들을 종합한 도출 예상은 다음과 같다. 정렬된 랜덤 쓰기에서 bs가 매핑 단위보다 작으면 사용자 데이터 대비 NAND 쓰기는 약 '매핑 단위/bs'배다(예: 16K 매핑에 4K 쓰기면 약 4배). GC가 시작되면 증폭은 더 커진다.

Throughput(BW/IOPS): Gemini 기록은 OS 기본 4KB 단위를 쓰는 워크로드에서 16KB 매핑이면 IOPS 하락이 필연적이라고 본다. Power_analysis에서는 16KB 미만 랜덤 쓰기의 바이트당 에너지(J/MB)가 크게 높아진다. 같은 데이터를 쓰는 데 내부 작업이 더 많다는 뜻이다. 16KB 이상의 정렬된 쓰기는 정상 수준이다. ZMS는 정렬 기법으로 랜덤 쓰기 성능이 5.0~13.6배 개선되었다고 보고하는데, 이는 비정렬 손실이 그만큼 크다는 점을 시사한다. 따라서 예상되는 경향은 이렇다. bs가 매핑 단위 이상인 구간에서는 매핑 단위 간 BW 차이가 작다. bs가 매핑 단위보다 작은 구간에서는 '매핑 단위/bs' 비율에 따라 BW가 떨어진다. 비교 실험인 4K 매핑에서는 모든 bs가 정렬 상태다.

Latency(clat): SFTL에 따르면 RMW는 이전 데이터를 먼저 읽기 때문에 쓰기 응답 시간을 늘린다. 불필요한 RMW 제거와 병합으로 쓰기 응답 시간이 최대 14%(평균 8%) 줄었고, 16KB MergeWindow에서는 최대 16%(평균 11%) 줄었다. 다만 병합에 실패하면 worst-case 지연은 늘어난다. Gemini 기록은 16KB 매핑에서 4KB 랜덤 I/O의 지연이 크게 늘고 P99 tail latency가 나빠진다고 본다. 반대로 매핑 단위를 키우면 맵이 메모리에 상주하기 쉬워져 map miss로 인한 읽기 지연은 줄어든다(ZMS: map miss 27.1%, 랜덤 읽기 37~44% 개선).
Energy/Power(참고용, NVMeVirt에서는 측정 불가): Power_analysis에 따르면 비정렬이거나 16KB 미만인 랜덤 쓰기는 평균 전력(W)이 같거나 오히려 낮다. RMW의 읽기가 쓰기보다 전력을 덜 쓰기 때문이다. 그러나 에너지(J/MB)는 크게 늘어난다. GC가 도는 dirty SSD에서는 쓰기 에너지가 더 늘어난다.
Read amplification: Gemini 기록에 따르면 RocksDB block_size가 4KB이고 SSD 매핑 단위가 16KB이면, 4KB만 필요해도 16KB를 읽게 된다. 그래서 block_size를 16KB로 맞추는 튜닝을 제안한다.

GC 전후 구분: Power_analysis는 clean과 dirty SSD를, ZMS는 clean과 aged 조건을 나눠 측정한다. 따라서 rand_time=0으로 GC 이전 구간을 포함해 측정하는 설계는 선행 연구의 방법과 맞는다. 도출 예상으로는, 큰 매핑 단위에서 작은 랜덤 쓰기가 들어오면 쓰기마다 page 하나를 통째로 소모하므로 GC 진입이 빨라지고, 진입 이후 성능 저하 폭도 커질 것이다.

[소스 외 검증 메모, NVMeVirt 코드 확인 결과] upstream NVMeVirt의 /home/dccearth/jsw/KSC2026/nvmevirt/upstream_tmp/conv_ftl.c 쓰기 경로(약 930~1010행)를 확인했다. start_lpn = lba / secs_per_pg로 계산하고, LPN마다 기존 ppa를 무효화한 뒤 새 page를 할당할 뿐이다. 매핑 단위보다 작은 쓰기에서도 기존 데이터에 대한 NAND read(RMW의 읽기 단계)는 하지 않는다. 즉 page 전체를 소모하는 데서 오는 공간·GC 증폭은 모델링되지만, 문헌이 말하는 RMW 읽기 지연은 모델링되지 않는다. 그래서 latency 저하가 문헌 기대보다 작게 나올 수 있다. 논문에 이 한계를 명시하거나, RMW read 시뮬레이션을 추가할지 결정해야 한다.

all_claims.title: CONFIRMED: when bs < MAP, conv_write allocates bs bytes per request but releases MAP bytes, so buffer->remaining grows without bound and write-buffer backpressure is gone from the start
all_claims.affects: All 15 cells with bs < MAP: MAP8K/bs4K; MAP16K/bs4K,8K; MAP32K/bs4K,8K,16K; MAP64K/bs4K..32K; MAP128K/bs4K..64K. The 21 cells with bs >= MAP are balanced.
all_claims.evidence:
Allocation is conv_ftl.c:961-963: buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)), which is exactly bs.

Pages written per request: start_lpn and end_lpn use secs_per_pg = MAP/512 (conv_ftl.c:937-938; ssd.c:73 as planned). With fio's default bs-aligned offsets and power-of-two sizes, a bs<MAP request touches exactly 1 LPN and a bs>=MAP request touches bs/MAP LPNs.

Release: on the last page of each wordline (conv_ftl.c:10-14, 1001-1008), schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz) releases ONESHOT bytes. pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT/pgsz (ssd.c:101), so the amortized release is pgsz = MAP per page written. The io worker performs the release with buffer_release (io.c:668-673).

No clamp exists: buffer_release does remaining += size with no min(size) (ssd.c:39-47). The only check is in buffer_allocate, 'remaining < size' (ssd.c:29-31). buffer_refill (ssd.c:49-55) has no caller in the conv path; grep finds only zns_mgmt_send.c:123.

Net per request = release - allocate = max(MAP,bs) - bs:
- MAP8K: +4K at bs4K
- MAP16K: +12K and +8K at bs4K/8K
- MAP32K: +28K, +24K, +16K at bs4K/8K/16K
- MAP64K: +60K, +56K, +48K, +32K at bs4K..32K
- MAP128K: +124K, +120K, +112K, +96K, +64K at bs4K..64K
- 0 for bs >= MAP

The release/allocate ratio is exactly MAP/bs (2x to 32x). acct.py replayed conv_write's lpn%4 partition and per-partition wordline logic over 50k random aligned requests and reproduced these numbers exactly.

Timed model (ftlsim.py, 0 allocation failures in every leaky case):
- MAP128K bs4K at 64K req/s: remaining goes from 4 MiB to 5.9 GB after 1 s and 33 GB after 20 s.
- MAP64K bs4K: 35 GB at 60 s.
- MAP32K bs4K: 23 GB at 60 s.
- MAP8K bs4K: 0.26 GB after 1 s.
The initial buffer (1-4 MiB) already covers the first-release delay of about 0.25-0.35 ms at these rates. Backpressure therefore never engages, even at t=0.
all_claims.impact_on_results:
In the 15 bs<MAP cells the buffer never throttles the host. The NAND/GC model still runs (each request programs a full MAP page: xfer_size = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg, conv_ftl.c:951), but because of early completion (see WB-3) none of it reaches fio. fio throughput and latency in these cells reflect emulator CPU speed (see WB-4), and later queue artifacts (see WB-2), not the mapping unit.

With the fix below, the same model gives:
- MAP128K bs4K: about 43.5K IOPS before GC (NAND-bound, 47.0K pages/s theoretical). GC starts at about 2.2 s; IOPS falls to 9.8K at 10 s and 5.0K at 30 s.
- MAP32K bs4K: 63.7K before GC (capped by the assumed 64K CPU rate). GC starts at 6.1 s; IOPS falls to 20.5K at 10 s and 10.3K at 30 s.
Unpatched, the model reports a flat 64K. The small-write penalty of large mapping units, the paper's key effect, is hidden or understated by up to about 10x in the GC phase.

all_claims.title: Consequence of WB-1: NAND backlog grows without bound, which overflows the 16384-entry io-worker queue (dropped commands, fio hang), hits the 393 ms channel-model horizon (printk storm, zero transfer time), and makes dispatcher/worker cost O(N)
all_claims.affects: bs<MAP cells whenever host page rate exceeds NAND page capacity. Before GC this is already the case for MAP64K and MAP128K at about 64K req/s. After GC starts it applies to effectively all 15 leaky cells.
all_claims.evidence:
One work-queue entry per programmed user wordline: conv_ftl.c:1007 calls schedule_internal_operation (io.c:357-388), which holds the entry until nsecs_target = NAND completion.

Capacity: NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO = 16384 per worker (nvmev.h:58). Internal ops go to the worker of req->sq_id, chosen by (sqid-1) % nr_io_workers (nvmev.h:12, io.c:25-32), so one fio job uses one worker. When the free list is exhausted, __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-304). Both internal ops (io.c:364-366) and host commands (io.c:325-327) are then silently dropped, after the FTL state was already updated. A dropped host command never gets a CQE, and the Admin Abort is a no-op with no CQE (admin.c:593-594), so the result is an nvme timeout and controller reset.

Cost per entry: __insert_req_sorted walks back from the tail over every entry with target > new target (io.c:264-274). That is O(N) per host command, since host targets are about now+5.6 us. The io-worker loop visits every entry and calls local_clock() each time (io.c:624-627), so each pass is O(N). At N = 16K, the insertion alone is at least about 16 us per command (at least 1 ns per dependent load), which already exceeds the whole 15.6 us per-command budget implied by 64K IOPS.

Channel horizon: chmodel_request with request_time - now >= 98304*4 us = 393.2 ms prints NVMEV_ERROR (printk KERN_ERR, nvmev.h:41) and returns request_time, i.e. zero transfer time (channel_model.c:71-77).

NAND page capacity before GC: MAP8K 285.8K/s, 16K 142.9K/s, 32K 71.5K/s, 64K 60.9K/s, 128K 47.0K/s. After GC it is divided by the write amplification, which the model puts at about 4-7 by 60 s.

ftlsim.py at bs=4K, open-loop 64K req/s (channel contention ignored, so these numbers are optimistic):

| MAP | GC onset | pending internal ops >= 16352 | LUN backlog > 393 ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 24.3 s | 38.5 s | 35.8 s |
| 16K | 12.1 s | 18.2 s | 17.3 s |
| 32K | 6.06 s | 6.79 s | 6.73 s |
| 64K | 3.03 s | 3.43 s | 3.29 s |
| 128K | 1.51 s | 0.96 s | 1.05 s |

In the baseline MAP4K/bs4K run, pending internal ops never exceeded 32.
all_claims.impact_on_results:
In leaky cells, results after a few seconds become one of two things:
- If the queue overflows: lost I/Os, a 30 s nvme timeout, and a possible controller reset. The run is invalid or hangs.
- If O(N) dispatcher and worker cost throttles the host first: host IOPS converges to whatever the pointer-chasing cost allows. That is a CPU-cache artifact, not an SSD parameter, and dmesg floods once backlog exceeds 393 ms.
Either way these data points cannot be interpreted. With bs < MAP for small bs, about half of the planned matrix is affected.
all_claims.suggested_fix:
Fixed by WB-1. With balanced accounting, pending internal ops are at most GLOBAL_WB_SIZE/ONESHOT = 32 for every MAP (the fixed-mode simulation shows max 32), and the LUN backlog stays at most about 24 ms.

After each run, also check dmesg for 'IO queue is almost full', 'Need to increase array size' and 'No free entry'. Treat any hit as an invalid run.

all_claims.title: With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 the host completion time never includes NAND or GC time. Foreground GC reaches fio only through write-buffer stalls and dispatcher CPU time.
all_claims.affects: All 36 cells. Determines how GC appears in the data.
all_claims.evidence:
Host completion: nsecs_xfer_completed = ssd_advance_write_buffer(nsecs_start, bs) = nsecs_start + 4000 + 460*ceil(bs/4K) + PCIe model (ssd.c:349-360; conv_ftl.c:965-967). conv_ftl.c:1015-1021 uses it unless FUA is set or early completion is off.

FUA never occurs here. fio direct=1 libaio does not set FUA, and the device reports vwc=0 (admin.c:431), so the block layer has no FUA or flush to pass.

GC path: credit exhaustion (conv_ftl.c:1011-1012) calls check_and_refill_write_credit (100-108), then foreground_gc, and do_gc(force) only if free_line_cnt <= 2 (815-822, 753-813). GC NAND commands use stime=0, i.e. now (ssd.c:365), and only advance lun->next_lun_avail_time (ssd.c:392, 417, 422-429, 435-437, 443-444).

The host's wordline program then starts at max(lun_avail, xfer_done) (ssd.c:422). Only its internal-op release time moves (conv_ftl.c:1004-1008), not ret->nsecs_target.

When the buffer is short, buffer_allocate fails, conv_write returns false (962-963), __nvmev_proc_io returns false (io.c:474-475), nvmev_proc_io_sq breaks without consuming the SQE (io.c:525-526, 538), and the dispatcher retries it on its next loop (main.c:145).
all_claims.impact_on_results:
In balanced cells (bs >= MAP), GC slowdown appears to fio only as buffer-full stalls. In the MAP4K/bs4K model, IOPS goes from 64K to about 28-37K after GC onset at about 48.6 s, and pending ops stay at most 32.

In leaky cells (WB-1), the buffer never fills, so GC's NAND cost is invisible to fio. Only the dispatcher CPU spent inside do_gc (see WB-5) shows up.

fio latency is wall-clock and includes SQ wait during stalls. NVMeVirt's modeled nsecs_start is re-sampled at each retry (io.c:444), so it excludes that wait.
all_claims.suggested_fix:
None needed for the balanced case. This is the intended model.

State it in the paper's method section, and apply WB-1 so GC becomes visible in all cells.

To also measure persistence-bound latency, an extra control run could use WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION 0 (ssd_config.h:106). Do not mix it into the main matrix.

all_claims.title: When the buffer does not throttle, the host bound is emulator CPU, not the SSD model. The model's own ceilings are the 3357 MiB/s PCIe credits and a 5.6-55.6 us latency floor.
all_claims.affects: All 15 leaky cells always. Balanced cells while CPU-bound before GC (for example MAP4K/bs4K).
all_claims.evidence:
PCIe model: 110 credits per 4 us slot x 128 B = 3.52e9 B/s (channel_model.h:160-162; channel_model.c:79-117), shared by all four partitions (conv_ftl.c:397-405).

Latency floor L(bs): see geometry. With QD32, Little's bound is 32/L: 5.7M IOPS at 4K and 576K at 128K, both above the PCIe cap. So the model's ceilings are: 4K 859K, 8K 430K, 16K 215K, 32K 107K, 64K 53.7K, 128K 26.9K IOPS.

The measured 64K IOPS (250 MiB/s) at MAP4K/bs4K is 13x below the model's 859K. That is CPU-bound:
- one polling dispatcher kthread does all FTL work for every SQ, including inline GC (main.c:167-189 and 138-148; io.c:441-508);
- one io worker per SQ does all memcpy (io.c:49-136, 634-656).

For balanced cells the NAND/PCIe ceiling before GC is: MAP<=32K 2233 MiB/s (NAND); MAP64K min(3805, 3357) = 3357 (PCIe); MAP128K min(5871, 3357) = 3357 (PCIe).
all_claims.impact_on_results: Small-bs cells, and all leaky cells, measure emulator CPU speed (CPU 3/4/5 performance, cache and IRQ path). Their absolute values will not transfer to another host, and differences between MAPs in those cells are not SSD effects.
all_claims.suggested_fix:
Report which cells are CPU-bound. A cell is CPU-bound if its IOPS is far below min(PCIe cap, NAND cap / write amplification).

After the WB-1 fix, small-bs/large-MAP cells become NAND-bound (for example MAP128K bs4K at about 43.5K IOPS before GC). They then become informative.

all_claims.title: Foreground GC runs synchronously on the dispatcher CPU. Its CPU time is the only GC effect fio can see in leaky cells, and it adds to buffer stalls in balanced cells.
all_claims.evidence:
conv_write calls consume_write_credit and check_and_refill_write_credit per page (conv_ftl.c:1011-1012, 93-108). When credits reach 0 and free_line_cnt <= 2, do_gc(force=true) runs inline (815-822).

Per GC, do_gc loops flashpgs_per_blk x 4 LUNs calls of clean_one_flashpg (773-807): 256 for MAP<=32K, 128 for 64K, 64 for 128K. Each scans pgs_per_flashpg pages twice (702-710, 729-739) and calls gc_write_page per valid page. That function does map/rmap updates, advance_write_pointer and ssd_advance_nand, which runs chmodel_request for program commands (598-643). mark_block_free scans pgs_per_blk pages per block (558-577).

Credits refill with victim->ipc (770, 106), so there is one GC per about ipc user pages per partition.

Modeled cumulative write amplification at 60 s (bs4K, unpatched): MAP8K 4.08, 16K 5.48, 32K 6.59, 64K 7.17. MAP128K reached 6.27 at 20 s. That is roughly 3-6 gc_write_page calls of dispatcher work per host write.
all_claims.impact_on_results:
In leaky cells, GC appears only as extra dispatcher CPU per request, a CPU-speed artifact. In balanced cells it is a minor addition to the buffer-stall effect.

This CPU time is real wall-clock even though NVMeVirt's model clocks treat GC as 'now'. GC CPU bursts can stall all SQs for the duration of one do_gc.
all_claims.suggested_fix:
No code change is needed for validity once WB-1 is fixed.

Optionally, log the GC count per run (for example a counter printed at rmmod) so the GC phase can be aligned with fio's time series.

all_claims.title: Setting FLASH_PAGE_SIZE = MAP for 64K and 128K changes the NAND model itself: per-die program bandwidth rises 1.70x/2.63x and the write buffer doubles or quadruples
all_claims.affects: Every cell with MAP64K or MAP128K, compared against MAP<=32K.
all_claims.evidence:
tPROG is a constant 185 us per one-shot page regardless of size (ssd_config.h:95; ssd.c:427-428). Channel transfer is ONESHOT/128 x 152 ns (ssd.c:424; channel_model.h:160).

Per-LUN wordline time and bandwidth: 32K 223.9 us (146 MB/s); 64K 262.8 us (249 MB/s); 128K 340.6 us (385 MB/s). Across 16 LUNs: 2233, 3805 and 5871 MiB/s.

GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*ONESHOT*2 (ssd_config.h:105) is 1, 2 and 4 MiB.

The assert that forces the change: ssd.c:98 requires (FLASH_PAGE_SIZE % pgsz) == 0.

GC reads use one tR (30-42 us) per flash page whatever its size (ssd.c:394-398), so GC read cost per byte also drops 2x/4x.

Net effect: with large bs before GC, MAP64K/128K become PCIe-bound at 3357 MiB/s while MAP<=32K are NAND-bound at 2233 MiB/s.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Any MAP64K/128K advantage at large bs, and part of their GC-phase behaviour, comes from a faster simulated NAND and a larger buffer, not from the mapping unit. Comparisons across the 32K to 64K boundary are confounded.
all_claims.suggested_fix:
Keep per-die program bandwidth constant across MAP. In the 970PRO block:

    #define NAND_PROG_LATENCY (185000 * (FLASH_PAGE_SIZE / KB(32)))

This gives 370 us at 64K and 740 us at 128K, so each one-shot page costs exactly 2x/4x the 32K wordline time.

Optionally scale NAND_READ_LATENCY_LSB/MSB the same way for GC reads.

If you prefer the user's 'page = mapping size' rule unchanged, at least document per-die bandwidth and buffer size per MAP in the report, and run a control MAP=32K cell with FLASH=64K.

all_claims.title: Sub-unit writes (bs < MAP) are modeled without read-modify-write: the old mapping unit is invalidated and a full new unit is programmed with no NAND read
all_claims.evidence:
In the conv_write loop (conv_ftl.c:971-1013), a mapped old ppa only triggers mark_page_invalid and set_rmap_ent(INVALID) (980-985). Then get_new_page and the program follow (988-1009). No NAND_READ of the remaining MAP-bs bytes is issued anywhere on the write path.

The data itself is kept correct by a byte-granular memcpy into the backing store (io.c:107-109), so this is purely a timing omission.
all_claims.impact_on_results: For large MAP, only the extra program bytes (MAP per request) are charged, not the merge read. Even after the WB-1 fix, the small-write penalty of large mapping units is underestimated: one extra tR plus a pgsz channel transfer per partial update, on the old page's LUN.

all_claims.title: Multi-partition (lpn % 4) effects: the leak ratio is unchanged, and release is merely delayed until each partition's open wordline fills
all_claims.affects: MAP4K/8K/16K, where pgs_per_oneshotpg > 1. All cells share one buffer.
all_claims.evidence:
Partition selection is conv_ftl.c:976-977. Each partition has its own write pointer and wordline (conv_ftl.c:984-998; struct conv_ftl wp in conv_ftl.h:58-68). One buffer and one PCIe model are shared by all four FTLs (conv_ftl.c:397-405). Each partition owns 2 channels and 4 LUNs (ssd.c:82-84).

Allocation held by partially filled wordlines in balanced cells is at most 4 x (ONESHOT - MAP): 112K at MAP4K, 96K at 8K, 64K at 16K. That is 11%, 9% and 6% of the 1 MiB buffer. It is 0 for MAP >= 32K.

When bs >= 4*MAP and requests are aligned, each request feeds all four partitions equally (for example MAP4K/bs128K gives 8 pages per partition, exactly one wordline each, releasing 128K for 128K allocated).

acct.py confirms the long-run release/allocate ratio is exactly max(1, MAP/bs) including the partition interleave.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Slightly reduces effective buffer depth for small MAP in balanced cells. It does not change the WB-1 conclusion.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None.

all_claims.title: io-worker selection is by SQ, so with numjobs=1 one worker does everything, and which one depends on the CPU fio runs on
all_claims.evidence:
nvmev.h:12 defines CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ, which makes __get_io_worker = (sqid-1) % nr_io_workers (io.c:25-32). nr_sq = min(host request, 72) (admin.c:495-496), so Linux gets one SQ per CPU.

Observed on this server: /proc/cpuinfo lists 6 CPUs and the cmdline has isolcpus=3-5, so fio runs on CPUs 0-2.

cpus=3,4,5 parsing: first entry is the dispatcher, the rest are workers (main.c:512-521). So worker0 is on CPU4 and worker1 on CPU5.

The nvmev_io_worker loop also does all memcpy for that SQ (io.c:634-656).
all_claims.impact_on_results: If fio migrates between CPUs 0-2, the active worker and work queue change during a run, which adds run-to-run variance. CPU 5 (or 4) is otherwise idle.
all_claims.suggested_fix:
Pin fio, for example with --cpus_allowed=1 or taskset -c 1, and record the pin in the report.

Optional: cpus=3,4 with one worker is equivalent for numjobs=1.

all_claims.title: GC onset time differs by a factor of about 30 across cells, so 60 s averages mix different fractions of pre-GC and GC phase
all_claims.evidence:
GC triggers after about 380 user lines per partition (conv_ftl.c:349-350, 370-371, 100-108, 815-822), i.e. about 12160 MiB of NAND pages. Host bytes before GC = 12160 MiB x min(1, bs/MAP).

Modeled onset at 64K req/s, bs4K: MAP4K 48.6 s; 8K 24.3 s; 16K 12.1 s; 32K 6.06 s; 64K 3.03 s; 128K 1.51 s.

For balanced cells running at the NAND cap of 2233 MiB/s, onset is at about 5.4 s.
all_claims.impact_on_results: A single 60 s mean per cell is not comparable between cells: some are mostly pre-GC, others mostly GC. Since ramp_time=0 is intended to capture both phases, they need to be separated.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Log per-second bandwidth and IOPS (fio --write_bw_log, --write_iops_log, --write_lat_log, --log_avg_msec=1000) and report pre-GC and steady GC phases separately. Record dmesg line counts per run.

all_claims.title: Planned geometry, asserts, MDTS and module parameters check out
all_claims.evidence:
- BLKS_PER_PLN=384 gives a 2048 KiB block for every MAP (ssd.c:86-107).
- The asserts at ssd.c:98-99 pass for FLASH=max(32K,MAP).
- The range check passes (conv_ftl.c:955-959).
- 128K I/O is within MDTS 256 KiB (ssd_config.h:70; pci.c:376; admin.c:435).
- memmap_start/size go through memparse (main.c:78-83). Storage = 12G - 1M (main.c:497-498).
- MAX_CH_XFER_SIZE only affects reads (ssd.c:404). It is irrelevant to this write workload.
- rmmod frees all FTL state and insmod rebuilds it: maps unmapped, lines free, LUN clocks 0, buffer full (conv_ftl.c:422-446, 376-420; ssd.c:14-19). So each run does start fresh.
all_claims.impact_on_results: No problem. Safe to record these values as the configuration in the report.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None.

verified.title: CONFIRMED: when bs < MAP, conv_write allocates bs bytes per request but releases MAP bytes, so buffer->remaining grows without bound and write-buffer backpressure is gone from the start
verified.affects: All 15 cells with bs < MAP: MAP8K/bs4K; MAP16K/bs4K,8K; MAP32K/bs4K,8K,16K; MAP64K/bs4K..32K; MAP128K/bs4K..64K. The 21 cells with bs >= MAP are balanced.
verified.evidence:
Allocation is conv_ftl.c:961-963: buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)), which is exactly bs.

Pages written per request: start_lpn and end_lpn use secs_per_pg = MAP/512 (conv_ftl.c:937-938; ssd.c:73 as planned). With fio's default bs-aligned offsets and power-of-two sizes, a bs<MAP request touches exactly 1 LPN and a bs>=MAP request touches bs/MAP LPNs.

Release: on the last page of each wordline (conv_ftl.c:10-14, 1001-1008), schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz) releases ONESHOT bytes. pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT/pgsz (ssd.c:101), so the amortized release is pgsz = MAP per page written. The io worker performs the release with buffer_release (io.c:668-673).

No clamp exists: buffer_release does remaining += size with no min(size) (ssd.c:39-47). The only check is in buffer_allocate, 'remaining < size' (ssd.c:29-31). buffer_refill (ssd.c:49-55) has no caller in the conv path; grep finds only zns_mgmt_send.c:123.

Net per request = release - allocate = max(MAP,bs) - bs:
- MAP8K: +4K at bs4K
- MAP16K: +12K and +8K at bs4K/8K
- MAP32K: +28K, +24K, +16K at bs4K/8K/16K
- MAP64K: +60K, +56K, +48K, +32K at bs4K..32K
- MAP128K: +124K, +120K, +112K, +96K, +64K at bs4K..64K
- 0 for bs >= MAP

The release/allocate ratio is exactly MAP/bs (2x to 32x). acct.py replayed conv_write's lpn%4 partition and per-partition wordline logic over 50k random aligned requests and reproduced these numbers exactly.

Timed model (ftlsim.py, 0 allocation failures in every leaky case):
- MAP128K bs4K at 64K req/s: remaining goes from 4 MiB to 5.9 GB after 1 s and 33 GB after 20 s.
- MAP64K bs4K: 35 GB at 60 s.
- MAP32K bs4K: 23 GB at 60 s.
- MAP8K bs4K: 0.26 GB after 1 s.
The initial buffer (1-4 MiB) already covers the first-release delay of about 0.25-0.35 ms at these rates. Backpressure therefore never engages, even at t=0.
verified.impact_on_results:
In the 15 bs<MAP cells the buffer never throttles the host. The NAND/GC model still runs (each request programs a full MAP page: xfer_size = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg, conv_ftl.c:951), but because of early completion (see WB-3) none of it reaches fio. fio throughput and latency in these cells reflect emulator CPU speed (see WB-4), and later queue artifacts (see WB-2), not the mapping unit.

With the fix below, the same model gives:
- MAP128K bs4K: about 43.5K IOPS before GC (NAND-bound, 47.0K pages/s theoretical). GC starts at about 2.2 s; IOPS falls to 9.8K at 10 s and 5.0K at 30 s.
- MAP32K bs4K: 63.7K before GC (capped by the assumed 64K CPU rate). GC starts at 6.1 s; IOPS falls to 20.5K at 10 s and 10.3K at 30 s.
Unpatched, the model reports a flat 64K. The small-write penalty of large mapping units, the paper's key effect, is hidden or understated by up to about 10x in the GC phase.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the path at upstream commit 61c90f7 and could not refute the claim. Every line it cites matches the source.

Allocation: conv_ftl.c:961-963 calls buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)), which is bs bytes. The pages written come from start_lpn and end_lpn at conv_ftl.c:937-938, which use secs_per_pg. With the planned edit, ssd.c:73 makes that MAP/512, and pgsz = MAP. An aligned bs<MAP request therefore covers exactly one LPN. The loop calls get_new_page for that LPN and maps a whole new MAP-sized page. There is no read-modify-write and no merging.

Release: last_pg_in_wordline (conv_ftl.c:10-14) fires once every pgs_per_oneshotpg pages, per partition. advance_write_pointer increments pg within a wordline before it moves to the next channel or LUN. On each firing, conv_ftl.c:1007-1008 schedules a release of pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz = ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE bytes. Since pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT/pgsz (ssd.c:101), the release averages out to MAP bytes per page written. The io worker applies it with buffer_release (io.c:670-673). GC writes never call schedule_internal_operation, so there are no other release paths, and buffer_allocate is the only allocation. buffer_release (ssd.c:39-47) does remaining += size with no clamp, and remaining is a size_t. buffer_refill is called only from zns_mgmt_send.c:123.

Backpressure: the only throttle is conv_write returning false. The dispatcher (__nvmev_proc_io and nvmev_proc_io_sq) then breaks out and retries the SQ entry later. That return happens only when remaining < bs. So for bs<MAP the net change per request is MAP-bs, and the ratio is MAP/bs. The numbers per cell (+4K … +124K) and the 15/21 split of the 36 cells are arithmetically right.

Initial buffer: GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*ONESHOT*2 = 32*ONESHOT. That is 1 MiB for MAP≤32K, 2 MiB for 64K and 4 MiB for 128K. This buffer covers far more requests than are in flight before the first release, which comes after about 0.2-0.35 ms of program time. Backpressure therefore never engages.

Early completion: with WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 and no FUA, ret->nsecs_target = nsecs_xfer_completed. That value comes from ssd_advance_write_buffer, which models only firmware and PCIe timing. NAND and GC timing reach the host only through the buffer, so the impact argument holds.

The proposed fix is consistent with the code. (end_lpn-start_lpn+1)*pgsz equals the amortized release for aligned requests. The early return happens before any FTL state changes, and 128K stays within the assert.

Minor imprecisions, none of which overturn the claim:
(1) The NVMEV_ASSERT limit at ssd.c:23 is buf->size = 32*ONESHOT, which is 1, 2 or 4 MiB depending on MAP. It is not a fixed 1 MiB. The fix is safe either way.
(2) "Grows without bound" and the ftlsim GB figures (e.g. 33 GB at 20 s) ignore the io-worker queue limit. NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO is 16384 entries per worker. When the host page rate exceeds the NAND rate (e.g. MAP128K bs4K: about 64K req/s against about 47K pages/s, and worse after GC starts), pending internal releases pile up until __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL. At that point both schedule_internal_operation (releases) and __enqueue_io_req (host completions) are silently dropped. remaining is already far larger than buf->size by then, so backpressure is still absent. However, the GB-scale numbers are a model idealization, and the real symptom becomes lost completions (the WB-2 artifact). The fix bounds this backlog as well.
(3) "None of it reaches fio" is slightly overstated. Foreground GC runs inline in conv_write on the dispatcher CPU (via consume/check_and_refill_write_credit), so GC's CPU cost does reach fio. GC's NAND timing does not.
verdicts.corrected_statement: The claim is confirmed. In conv_write, the write buffer is charged LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba) = bs per request (conv_ftl.c:961-963). It is credited ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE once per filled wordline (conv_ftl.c:1001-1008, io.c:670-673), which averages out to pgsz = MAP per page programmed. buffer_release has no clamp, and nothing in the conv path calls buffer_refill. So for every cell with bs < MAP (15 of the 36), remaining grows by MAP-bs per request and write-buffer backpressure never engages, not even at t=0. The 21 cells with bs >= MAP are balanced. The suggested fix restores balance: allocate (end_lpn-start_lpn+1)*pgsz and keep the bs-sized ssd_advance_write_buffer. Three refinements: (a) the assert limit is buf->size = 32*ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE (1, 2 or 4 MiB), not a fixed 1 MiB, and the fix stays within it in all cases. (b) In practice remaining does not grow literally without bound. Once the NAND backlog exceeds the io-worker queues (NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO = 16384 per worker), releases and host completions are silently dropped by __allocate_work_queue_entry. By then remaining already far exceeds buf->size, so backpressure is still absent, but the GB-scale ftlsim figures are idealized. (c) Foreground GC's CPU cost on the dispatcher still reaches fio; only GC's NAND timing is hidden.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked each step of the claim against upstream_tmp (61c90f7) and found no error.

1. Allocation. conv_ftl.c:961-963 calls buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)), which is exactly bs. The only check is ssd.c:29-31 (`remaining < size` sets size to 0). conv_write then returns false, io.c:474-475 returns false, and the SQ entry is retried. This retry is the only backpressure path.

2. Release. conv_ftl.c:1001-1008 runs only when last_pg_in_wordline (conv_ftl.c:10-14) is true. It calls schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz), which releases ONESHOT bytes. advance_write_pointer (conv_ftl.c:225-229) moves through pgs_per_oneshotpg pages of one wordline before switching channel or LUN. So in each of the 4 partitions, one wordline release happens per pgs_per_oneshotpg user pages, which averages pgsz = MAP bytes per page written. The io worker applies it with buffer_release (io.c:668-673). buffer_release (ssd.c:39-47) does `remaining += size` with no clamp. `remaining` is size_t (ssd.h:136), so it does not wrap. The only buffer_refill caller is zns_mgmt_send.c:123. GC writes (gc_write_page) never call schedule_internal_operation, so GC does not touch the buffer. The write buffer is shared across partitions (conv_ftl.c:401-404).

3. Worked examples.
- MAP=16K, bs=8K: secs_per_pg=32, FLASH=ONESHOT=32K, so pgs_per_oneshotpg=2. Request k has lba=16k and nr_lba=16, so start_lpn = end_lpn = floor(k/2): one LPN per request. Allocation is 8K. Each partition releases 32K per 2 pages, i.e. 16K per request. Net is +8K per request, matching the claim.
- MAP=8K, bs=4K: pgs_per_oneshotpg=4, release 32K per 4 pages = 8K per request, allocation 4K, net +4K. At 64K req/s that is +256 MB/s, matching the claimed 0.26 GB after 1 s. The NAND is not saturated here: about 70K 32K-wordlines/s across 16 LUNs.
- MAP=128K (FLASH=ONESHOT=128K), bs=4K: pgs_per_oneshotpg=1, so every request releases 128K and allocates 4K. Even when NAND-bound (~46-47K programs/s), release is about 6 GB/s against 0.26 GB/s allocated.
- Balanced case, MAP=4K, bs=8K: 2 LPNs per request, allocation 8K, release 8K. The 15 leaky and 21 balanced cells add up to 36, as claimed.

4. Initial buffer. GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*ONESHOT*2 (ssd_config.h:105). That is 1 MiB for MAP≤32K, 2 MiB for MAP=64K and 4 MiB for MAP=128K. This covers hundreds of 4K requests, which is far longer than the first-release delay of about 0.2-0.35 ms (tPROG 185 us plus channel transfer). So the allocate check never fails.

5. No other throttle. With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 (ssd_config.h:106), the host completion time is nsecs_xfer_completed: fw_wbuf latency plus PCIe (ssd.c:349-360), independent of NAND. Only the CPU cost of foreground GC on the dispatcher still reaches fio, which is consistent with the claim's 'emulator CPU speed' remark.

6. The proposed fix is sound. Allocating (end_lpn-start_lpn+1)*pgsz matches the average release for every (MAP, bs) pair, including unaligned requests that straddle two LPNs. The largest allocation, 128K, is at most the buffer size, which is at least 1 MiB, so it passes NVMEV_ASSERT(size <= buf->size) (ssd.c:23).

Two small caveats, neither of which changes the verdict:
- ftlsim's absolute GB figures (for example 33 GB at 20 s) come from a model, not from the code.
- When NAND completions drift into the future in the leaky MAP64K/128K cells, pending internal ops can fill the 16384-entry per-worker queue (nvmev.h:58). __allocate_work_queue_entry (io.c:301-304) then returns NULL, which silently drops releases and also drops host completions. This is the WB-2 artifact the claim points to. The fix bounds the number of outstanding wordlines by the buffer size, which also prevents this.
verdicts.corrected_statement: The claim is correct as stated. For bs < MAP, conv_write allocates bs bytes per request (conv_ftl.c:961), but over time the FTL releases ONESHOT/pgs_per_oneshotpg = MAP bytes per user page programmed (conv_ftl.c:1001-1008, io.c:671). buffer_release has no clamp and `remaining` is a 64-bit size_t. The net change per request is therefore +(MAP - bs). The write buffer (1/2/4 MiB at start) never refuses an allocation, and with early completion nothing from the NAND or GC model throttles fio, apart from the dispatcher's CPU time. This holds for all 15 cells with bs < MAP, and the 21 cells with bs >= MAP are balanced. The suggested fix restores balance for every (MAP, bs) pair and stays within the NVMEV_ASSERT limit: buf_bytes = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * spp->pgsz, with ssd_advance_write_buffer left at bs. The claim's GB trajectories come from a model, not from the code. In the leaky cells they can also be affected by internal ops dropped once the 16384-entry worker queue fills (io.c:301-304).

verified.title: Consequence of WB-1: NAND backlog grows without bound, which overflows the 16384-entry io-worker queue (dropped commands, fio hang), hits the 393 ms channel-model horizon (printk storm, zero transfer time), and makes dispatcher/worker cost O(N)
verified.affects: bs<MAP cells whenever host page rate exceeds NAND page capacity. Before GC this is already the case for MAP64K and MAP128K at about 64K req/s. After GC starts it applies to effectively all 15 leaky cells.
verified.evidence:
One work-queue entry per programmed user wordline: conv_ftl.c:1007 calls schedule_internal_operation (io.c:357-388), which holds the entry until nsecs_target = NAND completion.

Capacity: NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO = 16384 per worker (nvmev.h:58). Internal ops go to the worker of req->sq_id, chosen by (sqid-1) % nr_io_workers (nvmev.h:12, io.c:25-32), so one fio job uses one worker. When the free list is exhausted, __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-304). Both internal ops (io.c:364-366) and host commands (io.c:325-327) are then silently dropped, after the FTL state was already updated. A dropped host command never gets a CQE, and the Admin Abort is a no-op with no CQE (admin.c:593-594), so the result is an nvme timeout and controller reset.

Cost per entry: __insert_req_sorted walks back from the tail over every entry with target > new target (io.c:264-274). That is O(N) per host command, since host targets are about now+5.6 us. The io-worker loop visits every entry and calls local_clock() each time (io.c:624-627), so each pass is O(N). At N = 16K, the insertion alone is at least about 16 us per command (at least 1 ns per dependent load), which already exceeds the whole 15.6 us per-command budget implied by 64K IOPS.

Channel horizon: chmodel_request with request_time - now >= 98304*4 us = 393.2 ms prints NVMEV_ERROR (printk KERN_ERR, nvmev.h:41) and returns request_time, i.e. zero transfer time (channel_model.c:71-77).

NAND page capacity before GC: MAP8K 285.8K/s, 16K 142.9K/s, 32K 71.5K/s, 64K 60.9K/s, 128K 47.0K/s. After GC it is divided by the write amplification, which the model puts at about 4-7 by 60 s.

ftlsim.py at bs=4K, open-loop 64K req/s (channel contention ignored, so these numbers are optimistic):

| MAP | GC onset | pending internal ops >= 16352 | LUN backlog > 393 ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 24.3 s | 38.5 s | 35.8 s |
| 16K | 12.1 s | 18.2 s | 17.3 s |
| 32K | 6.06 s | 6.79 s | 6.73 s |
| 64K | 3.03 s | 3.43 s | 3.29 s |
| 128K | 1.51 s | 0.96 s | 1.05 s |

In the baseline MAP4K/bs4K run, pending internal ops never exceeded 32.
verified.impact_on_results:
In leaky cells, results after a few seconds become one of two things:
- If the queue overflows: lost I/Os, a 30 s nvme timeout, and a possible controller reset. The run is invalid or hangs.
- If O(N) dispatcher and worker cost throttles the host first: host IOPS converges to whatever the pointer-chasing cost allows. That is a CPU-cache artifact, not an SSD parameter, and dmesg floods once backlog exceeds 393 ms.
Either way these data points cannot be interpreted. With bs < MAP for small bs, about half of the planned matrix is affected.
verified.suggested_fix:
Fixed by WB-1. With balanced accounting, pending internal ops are at most GLOBAL_WB_SIZE/ONESHOT = 32 for every MAP (the fixed-mode simulation shows max 32), and the LUN backlog stays at most about 24 ms.

After each run, also check dmesg for 'IO queue is almost full', 'Need to increase array size' and 'No free entry'. Treat any hit as an invalid run.

verdicts.reasoning:
The code mechanics check out line by line in upstream_tmp at 61c90f7:
- conv_ftl.c:1007 queues one internal op per programmed user wordline. Its target is the NAND completion time (ssd.c NAND_WRITE).
- schedule_internal_operation (io.c:357) and __enqueue_io_req both return silently when __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-304, 325-327, 364-366). - __insert_req_sorted walks back from the tail over every entry whose target is later than the new one (io.c:266-274). A host target is about now+5.6 us, so that walk is O(N).
- The worker loop visits every entry and calls local_clock() each time (io.c:624-627).
- chmodel_request prints NVMEV_ERROR and returns request_time when the offset is >= 98304*4 us (channel_model.c:71-77).
- Admin Abort is a no-op with no CQE (admin.c:593-594).
- The buffer is leaky when bs < MAP: it allocates bs bytes per write but releases pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz per wordline, and remaining is a size_t.
- One worker: the device gets only "1/0/0 default/read/poll queues", so all I/O uses sqid 1, which maps to worker 0.

The predicted consequences are contradicted by base-variant runs on this server. That build has WBUF_FIX=0, and io.c, channel_model.c and the buffer code are identical to upstream (results/main_20261008/base):
(1) Before GC the backlog is bounded, not unbounded, and the host rate is not about 64K/s. The 500 ms fio IOPS samples sit exactly at the modelled NAND page capacity:

  - Only the first 0.5 s runs higher (291K and 149K). From that excess, the equilibrium backlog is roughly 0.7K-1.5K internal ops, far below 16K.

(2) The queue did not overflow and fio did not hang. Both runs ended at about 60.3 s with fio_exit 0, and no WARNING was logged.
(3) GC started at about 5.7 s (the simulation said 24.3 s and 12.1 s), and the 393 ms horizon was hit at about 16-17 s (it said 35.8 s and 17.3 s).
  - After that, KERN_ERR messages piled up: 8.24M for MAP8K and 6.76M for MAP16K, with journald reporting /dev/kmsg overruns.
  - IOPS fell to about 34K for MAP8K and was still falling (to about 20K) for MAP16K.
