all_claims.title: Write-buffer accounting is asymmetric when bs < MAP: flow control disappears and the device can stop completing commands
all_claims.affects: Every (MAP, bs) pair with bs < MAP: 15 of the 36 combinations, e.g. MAP=8K bs=4K up to MAP=128K bs=4K..64K. Pairs with bs >= MAP are unaffected.
all_claims.evidence: conv_write takes from the buffer only the bytes the host sent: allocated_buf_size = buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)) (conv_ftl.c:961-963). It gives back a whole oneshot page each time one is programmed: schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz) (conv_ftl.c:1001-1009). buffer_release does 'remaining += size' with no upper limit (ssd.c:39-47). A bs<MAP request covers 1 lpn, so it takes bs bytes and in time returns MAP bytes. remaining therefore grows by (MAP-bs) per request and goes past buf->size after a few hundred requests, so the check 'remaining < size' (ssd.c:29-31) never fails again. With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 the host completion time is nsecs_xfer_completed, which is firmware + PCIe time only (conv_ftl.c:965-967, 1015-1021; ssd.c:349-360). NAND time no longer reaches the host at all. When NAND demand exceeds capacity, lun->next_lun_avail_time keeps moving further into the future. Capacity in programs/s is 16/cycle: 71,457 for FLASH 32K, 60,878 for 64K, 46,970 for 128K; for MAP=128K bs=4K at the ~64K IOPS measured on this server, demand already exceeds it before any GC. Two failures follow. (a) Every internal release op waits in the worker queue until its NAND completion time. Pending ops exceed NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO=16384 (nvmev.h:58) once the backlog passes 16384/capacity = 0.23 s / 0.27 s / 0.35 s. The queue is per worker, and with one SQ all ops go to the same worker (io.c:28). Then __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-303) and __enqueue_io_req returns without queuing the host command (io.c:325-327), so that command never gets a completion and fio hangs or hits nvme timeouts. (b) Past NR_CREDIT_ENTRIES*4 us = 393 ms ahead, chmodel_request prints 'Need to increase array size' and returns request_time, i.e. zero channel time (channel_model.c:73-76; channel_model.h:7-8).
all_claims.impact_on_results: For bs<MAP, IOPS and bandwidth show only the dispatcher CPU / firmware / PCIe path, not the MAP/bs program amplification, so the sub-page penalty the paper wants to measure is hidden. Later in a run, once GC starts, the device can drop commands, give I/O errors, or leave fio stuck. These data points are not valid.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Take from the buffer what is actually programmed. In conv_write: 'size_t need = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * spp->pgsz; allocated_buf_size = buffer_allocate(wbuf, need); if (allocated_buf_size < need) return false;'. need is at most 128K, which is <= WB, so the assert at ssd.c:23 still holds. Optionally also cap remaining at buf->size in buffer_release (ssd.c:43). Alternatively run only bs >= MAP. After every run, grep dmesg for 'IO queue is almost full', 'Need to increase array size' and 'No free line left' and throw out runs that show them.

all_claims.title: Making FLASH_PAGE_SIZE 64K/128K while tPROG/tR stay fixed raises NAND bandwidth 1.7x / 2.6x (confound between MAP<=32K and MAP 64K/128K)
all_claims.affects: Any comparison between MAP in {4K..32K} (FLASH 32K) and MAP in {64K, 128K} (FLASH = MAP). Strongest at large bs and after GC starts.
all_claims.evidence: A NAND write is one channel transfer of the whole oneshot page followed by a fixed tPROG: chmodel_request(ch, chnl_stime, ncmd->xfer_size), then nand_etime = nand_stime + spp->pg_wr_lat (ssd.c:420-431). xfer_size = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT (conv_ftl.c:951). pg_wr_lat = NAND_PROG_LATENCY = 185000 ns for every page size (ssd_config.h:95; ssd.c:117). Channel cost is 152 ns per 128 B (channel_model.h:40, BANDWIDTH_TO_TX_TIME(800)). Per-die cycle: 32K = 38,912+185,000 = 223,912 ns, i.e. 139.6 MiB/s. 64K = 262,824 ns, i.e. 237.8 MiB/s. 128K = 340,648 ns, i.e. 366.9 MiB/s. Across 16 dies the ceilings are 2,233 / 3,805 / 5,871 MiB/s. The host write path also passes the shared PCIe model at 3360 (ssd.c:349-360; conv_ftl.c:397-405), about 3,357 MiB/s. So MAP<=32K is NAND-bound at about 2.23 GiB/s while MAP 64K/128K is PCIe-bound at about 3.3 GiB/s. GC reads are affected the same way: tR is fixed (NAND_READ_LATENCY ~30/42 us at ssd_config.h:92-93, chosen at ssd.c:394-398), so each 64K/128K flash-page read moves 2x/4x more data for the same sensing time.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Higher bandwidth or smaller GC slowdown at MAP 64K/128K can come from the bigger NAND page, not from the mapping unit. The step between MAP=32K and MAP=64K cannot be attributed to MAP.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Option 1: keep bandwidth per byte constant by scaling the latencies with FLASH/32K. NAND_PROG_LATENCY becomes 370000 (64K) and 740000 (128K), which reproduces 139.6 MiB/s per die exactly because the transfer scales linearly too: 65536/(77,824+370,000) = 32768/223,912. Scale NAND_READ_LATENCY_* by the same factor. Option 2: use one NAND geometry for all six MAPs, e.g. FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=KB(128), which satisfies the ssd.c:98 assert for every MAP <= 128K. Either way, state the choice in the document.

all_claims.title: The NVMeVirt target must be found by model string; the root filesystem is on nvme0n1
all_claims.affects: All runs (operational safety of the fio scripts)
all_claims.evidence: lsblk on this host shows nvme0n1 = 'Samsung SSD 980 PRO 500GB' with / and /boot/efi mounted on it. The emulated controller reports mn='CSL_Virt_MN_01' and sn='CSL_Virt_SN_01' (admin.c:432-433). The controller and namespace number are assigned by the kernel at every insmod, and the plan does an rmmod/insmod before each of its runs.
all_claims.impact_on_results: A hard-coded or wrong device in a randwrite job with direct=1 over the whole device would wipe the root disk. A device that silently changes name would also mix up results.
all_claims.suggested_fix: After each insmod, find the device by model, e.g. 'for d in /sys/block/nvme*n1; do grep -q CSL_Virt "$d/device/model" && echo /dev/${d##*/}; done'. Abort if the result is not exactly one device. Record the resolved name, its size in bytes (expect 12040984064) and max_hw_sectors_kb in the log.

all_claims.title: MAP=64K/128K with FLASH_PAGE_SIZE still at 32K fails ssd.c:98 with BUG_ON at insmod
all_claims.affects: MAP=64K and 128K builds in which ssd_config.h:77 was not changed
all_claims.evidence: NVMEV_ASSERT is BUG_ON(!(x)) (nvmev.h:42). ssd.c:98 is NVMEV_ASSERT((ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE % spp->pgsz) == 0 && (FLASH_PAGE_SIZE % spp->pgsz) == 0). With FLASH=ONESHOT=32768 and pgsz=65536, 32768 % 65536 = 32768, so it fires inside module init (conv_init_namespace → ssd_init_params, called from NVMeV_init at main.c:628). With the planned FLASH=MAP: 65536%65536 = 0 and 131072%131072 = 0, so it passes. For MAP<=32K, 32768 % MAP = 0.
all_claims.impact_on_results: A wrong build oopses the kernel during insmod. The module stays stuck in its init state and the server must be rebooted, which breaks an unattended 108-run batch.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Build one nvmev.ko per MAP ahead of time (e.g. nvmev_map64k.ko). Record each one's ssd_config.h/ssd.c diff and md5sum. Before insmod, check with 'strings' or a modinfo tag that the module matches the MAP being run.

all_claims.title: Write-buffer size and wordline aggregation change with MAP/FLASH
all_claims.affects: Comparisons across MAP (4K..32K vs 64K vs 128K) and across bs
all_claims.evidence: GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = NAND_CHANNELS*LUNS_PER_NAND_CH*ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE*2 (ssd_config.h:105, assigned at ssd.c:130) gives 1 MiB for MAP<=32K, 2 MiB for 64K and 4 MiB for 128K. It is one buffer shared by all 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:397-405). Measured in oneshot programs it stays at 32, i.e. 2 per die, so the backpressure depth in programs is constant, but the bytes the host can have queued double and then quadruple. pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT/pgsz (ssd.c:101) is 8/4/2/1/1/1. A NAND program starts only on the last page of a wordline (conv_ftl.c:10-14, 1001-1009). So at MAP=4K each partition must collect 8 lpns before programming, while MAP>=32K programs on every lpn. At MAP=4K bs=4K the buffer can hold up to 4 partitions x 7 x 4K = 112 KiB of partly filled wordlines.
all_claims.impact_on_results: These are model parameters that change along with MAP. They have to be disclosed, and they partly explain throughput and latency differences.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Report WB bytes and pgs_per_oneshotpg for each MAP in the experiment record. If both C2 and C5 must be removed, a single FLASH=ONESHOT=128K for all MAPs fixes WB at 4 MiB.

all_claims.title: Sub-page writes are not modelled as read-modify-write
all_claims.evidence: For each lpn, conv_write only invalidates the old PPA, takes a new page and updates the map (conv_ftl.c:971-998). It never issues a NAND_READ for the (MAP-bs) bytes the host did not write. Data stays correct only because the payload is copied by byte offset into the backing memory (io.c:107-109).
all_claims.impact_on_results: The sub-page penalty consists only of program amplification (MAP/bs NAND bytes per host byte) plus earlier GC. The tR + transfer of a real RMW is missing, so the penalty for small bs at large MAP is underestimated (in addition to C1).
all_claims.suggested_fix: State this as a limitation. Alternatively, for a partially covered lpn that is already mapped, issue a NAND_READ of the old PPA (xfer=pgsz) before the program and use its completion time as swr.stime.

all_claims.title: The mapping table is a flat host-memory array with no mapping-cache (DFTL/CMT) model
all_claims.evidence: get_maptbl_ent/set_maptbl_ent index conv_ftl->maptbl[lpn] directly (conv_ftl.c:26-35). The table is vmalloc'd with tt_pgs entries of 8 B (conv_ftl.c:300-309); rmap is another 8 B per page (conv_ftl.c:316-325). No code path charges NAND time for map pages. Sizes (all 4 partitions): maptbl 24 / 12 / 6 / 3 / 1.5 / 0.75 MiB and rmap the same, for MAP 4K..128K.
all_claims.impact_on_results: The DRAM-footprint argument for a larger MAP (24 MiB down to 0.75 MiB of L2P at 11.2 GiB) shows up nowhere in the performance numbers. The MAP effects that are modelled are wordline aggregation, sub-page program amplification, GC granularity, and the dispatcher's per-lpn CPU cost.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Report L2P size analytically from tt_pgs*8 B, and do not attribute any performance difference to mapping-table size.

all_claims.title: GC onset in the 60 s window depends on MAP, bs and throughput; ramp_time=0 averages pre-GC and GC phases
all_claims.affects: All runs; how much each average is distorted differs per (MAP, bs)
all_claims.evidence: tt_lines=384 per partition. 2 lines are reserved at init (conv_ftl.c:349-350). foreground_gc runs only when free_line_cnt <= gc_thres_lines_high=2 (conv_ftl.c:21-24, 371, 815-822), checked every pgs_per_line user pages (conv_ftl.c:100-108, 159-160). The first GC therefore follows 380 x 8 MiB x 4 = 12,160 MiB of page writes, which is 1.059x the exported 11,483 MiB. For bs >= MAP that equals 12,160 MiB of host writes: 48.6 s at the measured 250 MiB/s, 5.4 s at 2,233 MiB/s, 3.6 s at 3,357 MiB/s. For bs < MAP it is 12,160 x bs/MAP MiB, e.g. 380 MiB for MAP=128K bs=4K. Also, fio's default random map (norandommap=0) writes every block exactly once per pass. So for bs >= MAP no page is invalid until 11,483 MiB have been written, and at GC onset the victim lines are still about 94% valid (677/11,483 invalidated), which gives a sharp cliff. randrepeat=1 (the default) makes all 3 repetitions use the same LBA sequence.
all_claims.impact_on_results: A 60-s mean bandwidth mixes FOB and GC regimes in proportions that differ per configuration, so means are hard to compare. The 3 repetitions capture emulator timing noise only, not workload variation.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Add write_bw_log/write_iops_log/write_lat_log with log_avg_msec=1000, and report the pre-GC and post-GC phases separately (the onset is visible in the 1-s log). Record norandommap and randrepeat explicitly; consider randseed=<rep> to vary the sequence. Optionally run long enough to reach steady state, or precondition, if steady-state numbers are wanted.

all_claims.title: 128K requests are not split: MDTS=6 with MPSMIN=0 allows 256 KiB
all_claims.evidence: MDTS (6) in ssd_config.h:70 becomes nvmev_vdev->mdts (main.c:561), then ctrl->mdts (admin.c:435). CAP.MPSMIN = 0, i.e. 4 KiB pages (pci.c:376). Maximum transfer = 2^6 x 4 KiB = 256 KiB, so Linux sets max_hw_sectors to 512 sectors. The identify-namespace page is zeroed (admin.c:274), so NOIOB=0 and there is no boundary split. Transfers use PRP lists only, and io.c:77-90 handles a single PRP-list page (up to 512 entries), enough for 32 pages. LBA format 512 B (flbas=0, admin.c:304-305). buffer_allocate's assert size <= buf->size (ssd.c:23) holds: 128K <= 1 MiB.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Each 128k fio I/O becomes exactly one NVMe command. bs=128k is valid.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None. After insmod, record /sys/block/<virt>/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb (expect 256) and max_sectors_kb. Note that the real nvme0n1 reports 128, so do not confuse the two devices.

all_claims.title: Every init assert and static_assert passes for the planned six configurations
all_claims.evidence: static_assert ONESHOT%FLASH==0 (ssd_config.h:81) passes with ONESHOT=FLASH*1. ssd.c:82: 8%4==0. ssd.c:92 is not reached because BLKS_PER_PLN>0. ssd.c:98: 32K%{4,8,16,32}K==0, 64K%64K==0, 128K%128K==0. ssd.c:99 passes. conv_ftl.c:118: lm->tt_lines(384)==spp->tt_lines(384). conv_ftl.c:143 passes. conv_ftl.c:201-202 pass with 382 free lines after the two wp grabs. PPA bitfields PAGE_BITS=16 and BLK_BITS=16 (ssd.h:53-58) fit pgs_per_blk<=512 and blks<=384. Every host lpn is in range: max local lpn < tt_pgs for every MAP (e.g. 734,923 < 786,432 at 4K, 22,966 < 24,576 at 128K), so the 'lpn passed FTL range' rejection (conv_ftl.c:955-959) never fires. set_maptbl_ent and ppa2pgidx asserts (conv_ftl.c:33,48) hold. The int loop counters in init_maptbl/init_rmap (conv_ftl.c:302-308) reach at most 786,432.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Each configuration will load and run, apart from the runtime failure mode in C1.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None

all_claims.title: Block is exactly 2 MiB and exported capacity and OP are identical for every MAP
all_claims.evidence: blk_size = DIV_ROUND_UP(3,220,963,328, 1536) = 2,096,982 (ssd.c:86-90). oneshotpgs_per_blk = DIV_ROUND_UP(2,096,982, ONESHOT) = 64/32/16 (ssd.c:102), so pgs_per_blk*pgsz = 2,097,152 B (ssd.c:107,165). Modeled NAND = 12,288 MiB, 1 MiB above storage_size (main.c:498). That is harmless: data is stored by LBA offset (io.c:109), and ns->size comes from storage_size*100/107 = 12,040,984,403 B (conv_ftl.c:373,411). nsze = 23,517,547 LBAs = 12,040,984,064 B (admin.c:315-317). Effective OP = 7.01%, about 25.1 spare 8-MiB lines per partition, for every MAP.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Capacity and OP do not confound MAP. The user's 'BLKS_PER_PLN=384 gives 2 MiB' is confirmed.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None. Record the dmesg lines 'Total Capacity...blk-size(MiB,KiB)=2,2048 line-size(MiB,KiB)=8,8192' and 'FTL physical space: 12883853312, logical space: 12040984403' for each run.

all_claims.title: MAX_CH_XFER_SIZE=16K is not a confound for writes
all_claims.evidence: The MAX_CH_XFER_SIZE chunking loop exists only in NAND_READ (ssd.c:403-415). NAND_WRITE moves the whole oneshot page with one chmodel_request (ssd.c:424). GC reads use interleave_pci_dma=false (conv_ftl.c:719-724), and chunking adds no time because channel latency is linear in 128-B units (channel_model.c:117). Channel load from 2 LUNs per channel: 2x38.9/223.9 = 35% (32K), 2x77.8/262.8 = 59% (64K), 2x155.6/340.6 = 91% (128K). At 128K the channel is close to saturated but not the bottleneck.
all_claims.impact_on_results: No effect on randwrite numbers apart from what C2 already covers.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None

all_claims.title: With IO_WORKER_BY_SQ and numjobs=1, only one of the two I/O workers does the work
all_claims.evidence: cpus=3,4,5 gives dispatcher CPU 3 and workers on CPUs 4 and 5 (main.c:512-521). CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ is defined (nvmev.h:12), so worker = (sqid-1) % nr_io_workers (io.c:28). Internal buffer-release ops use req->sq_id as well (conv_ftl.c:1007). The host has 6 logical CPUs (nproc --all = 6) and isolcpus=3-5, so fio runs on CPUs 0-2, and which SQ (and therefore which worker) it uses depends on the CPU it lands on.
all_claims.impact_on_results: There is effectively 1 worker, not 2, and the active worker can differ between repetitions, adding variance to the memcpy and completion path.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Pin fio (cpus_allowed=0, or taskset -c 0) and record that. Describe the CPU setup in the paper as '1 dispatcher + 1 active worker (per-SQ assignment)'.

all_claims.title: Large unchecked kmalloc/vmalloc count at insmod, worst at MAP=4K
all_claims.evidence: ssd_init_nand_page does one kmalloc of secs_per_pg*4 B per page (ssd.c:174-183). That is tt_pgs allocations per insmod: 3,145,728 at 4K and 98,304 at 128K, 96 MiB total in every case. Add 16 B/page nand_page arrays (ssd.c:194) and maptbl+rmap vmalloc (conv_ftl.c:305,321): about 192 MiB at 4K and 99 MiB at 128K. None of these allocations is NULL-checked, and neither is the ~96 KiB channel_model kmalloc (ssd.c:265,286; struct at channel_model.h:29-38).
all_claims.impact_on_results: Fine with about 12 GB of free RAM. Over 108 insmod/rmmod cycles, an order-5 kmalloc failure would show up as an oops rather than an error.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Check 'free -m' and dmesg after each insmod. No code change needed.

all_claims.title: rmmod/insmod fully resets the FTL; idle timers cost at most 1 jiffy at the start
all_claims.evidence: NVMeV_exit calls conv_remove_namespace, which frees maptbl, rmap, lines and ssd (main.c:657-670; conv_ftl.c:422-446). On load, every line is free and every page PG_FREE (conv_ftl.c:128-141; ssd.c:182), so each run starts fresh-out-of-box. The reserved memory is not zeroed, which does not matter for write-only runs. The static last_io_time / last_dispatched_time start at 0 (io.c:604; main.c:169), so the threads sleep 1 jiffy per loop until the first I/O or doorbell (io.c:730-734; main.c:181-185).
all_claims.impact_on_results: FOB start is guaranteed. The idle-timer effect is limited to the first I/O.
all_claims.suggested_fix: None. Keep 'rmmod nvmev; insmod ...; wait for udev settle; resolve device (C3); start fio' and log dmesg for each run.

verified.title: Write-buffer accounting is asymmetric when bs < MAP: flow control disappears and the device can stop completing commands
verified.affects: Every (MAP, bs) pair with bs < MAP: 15 of the 36 combinations, e.g. MAP=8K bs=4K up to MAP=128K bs=4K..64K. Pairs with bs >= MAP are unaffected.
verified.evidence: conv_write takes from the buffer only the bytes the host sent: allocated_buf_size = buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)) (conv_ftl.c:961-963). It gives back a whole oneshot page each time one is programmed: schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz) (conv_ftl.c:1001-1009). buffer_release does 'remaining += size' with no upper limit (ssd.c:39-47). A bs<MAP request covers 1 lpn, so it takes bs bytes and in time returns MAP bytes. remaining therefore grows by (MAP-bs) per request and goes past buf->size after a few hundred requests, so the check 'remaining < size' (ssd.c:29-31) never fails again. With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 the host completion time is nsecs_xfer_completed, which is firmware + PCIe time only (conv_ftl.c:965-967, 1015-1021; ssd.c:349-360). NAND time no longer reaches the host at all. When NAND demand exceeds capacity, lun->next_lun_avail_time keeps moving further into the future. Capacity in programs/s is 16/cycle: 71,457 for FLASH 32K, 60,878 for 64K, 46,970 for 128K; for MAP=128K bs=4K at the ~64K IOPS measured on this server, demand already exceeds it before any GC. Two failures follow. (a) Every internal release op waits in the worker queue until its NAND completion time. Pending ops exceed NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO=16384 (nvmev.h:58) once the backlog passes 16384/capacity = 0.23 s / 0.27 s / 0.35 s. The queue is per worker, and with one SQ all ops go to the same worker (io.c:28). Then __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-303) and __enqueue_io_req returns without queuing the host command (io.c:325-327), so that command never gets a completion and fio hangs or hits nvme timeouts. (b) Past NR_CREDIT_ENTRIES*4 us = 393 ms ahead, chmodel_request prints 'Need to increase array size' and returns request_time, i.e. zero channel time (channel_model.c:73-76; channel_model.h:7-8).
verified.impact_on_results: For bs<MAP, IOPS and bandwidth show only the dispatcher CPU / firmware / PCIe path, not the MAP/bs program amplification, so the sub-page penalty the paper wants to measure is hidden. Later in a run, once GC starts, the device can drop commands, give I/O errors, or leave fio stuck. These data points are not valid.
verified.suggested_fix: Take from the buffer what is actually programmed. In conv_write: 'size_t need = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * spp->pgsz; allocated_buf_size = buffer_allocate(wbuf, need); if (allocated_buf_size < need) return false;'. need is at most 128K, which is <= WB, so the assert at ssd.c:23 still holds. Optionally also cap remaining at buf->size in buffer_release (ssd.c:43). Alternatively run only bs >= MAP. After every run, grep dmesg for 'IO queue is almost full', 'Need to increase array size' and 'No free line left' and throw out runs that show them.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced every cited line in /home/dccearth/jsw/KSC2026/nvmevirt/upstream_tmp at commit 61c90f7 and the mechanism holds.

Allocate side, conv_ftl.c:961-963: buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba)) takes host bytes, so a bs-aligned request with bs<MAP takes bs bytes. In that case start_lpn == end_lpn, so it covers one lpn.

Release side, conv_ftl.c:1001-1009: when last_pg_in_wordline() is true (conv_ftl.c:10-14), conv_write calls schedule_internal_operation(..., pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz). The worker runs buffer_release only once w->nsecs_target, the NAND completion time, has passed (io.c:668-672). Each programmed lpn therefore returns pgsz = MAP bytes on average.

buffer_release (ssd.c:39-47) does remaining += size with no cap. So remaining = WB - N*bs + P*MAP, where N is the number of requests and P the number of lpns whose program has completed. The check at ssd.c:29-31 can only fail if the host's byte rate exceeds the NAND program byte rate, which is programs/s x ONESHOT, roughly 2.3 to 6.2 GB/s. A ~250 MB/s workload never gets there, so for bs<MAP remaining passes buf->size almost at once and the throttle never fires again.

The write buffer is one object shared by all 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:401-404). GLOBAL_WB_SIZE is 32*ONESHOT (ssd_config.h:103). With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1, ret->nsecs_target = nsecs_xfer_completed (conv_ftl.c:1015-1021), which is fw_wbuf_lat0 + lat1 + PCIe (ssd.c:349-360). GC writes (gc_write_page, conv_ftl.c:596-631) move lun->next_lun_avail_time forward but never touch the buffer. In this configuration the buffer is the only path from NAND time back to the host.

Capacity figures are confirmed. xfer_lat = 128e9/MB(800) = 152 ns per 128 B and FW_CH_XFER_LATENCY = 0. A program cycle is 256*152+185000 ns for 32K, giving 71,457/s; 60,878/s for 64K; 46,970/s for 128K, across 16 LUNs.

(a) is confirmed. nvmev.h:12 defines CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ, so __get_io_worker = (sqid-1)%nr_io_workers (io.c:27-28). If __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-303), __enqueue_io_req returns (io.c:325-327). __nvmev_proc_io still returns true, so the SQ entry is consumed and never completed (io.c:482, 523-535). NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO is 16384 (nvmev.h:58).

(b) is confirmed. NR_CREDIT_ENTRIES = 98304 times 4 us is 393 ms. Beyond that, chmodel_request prints NVMEV_ERROR "Need to increase array size" and returns request_time (channel_model.c:73-76).

The 15-of-36 count is correct.

Three inaccuracies or omissions, none of which reverses the claim:
1. The dmesg check in the suggested fix will not work for one string. io.c:302 is WARN_ON_ONCE("IO queue is almost full"). The string literal is the condition, so the kernel prints a generic "WARNING: ... at io.c:302 __allocate_work_queue_entry" once per module load, and the text "IO queue is almost full" never appears in dmesg.
2. "NAND time never reaches the host" is true of the timing model, but not of the host's view overall. __insert_req_sorted (io.c:257-268) walks backward from the queue tail past every not-yet-due entry. Every host completion has a near-term target, so each one walks past all pending future-dated release ops. Dispatcher cost per command therefore grows linearly with the NAND backlog. That pushes IOPS down as the backlog grows, but it is an artifact of the emulator's CPU cost, not modeled NAND timing. It may also hold the backlog below 16384, so failure (a) is a real risk that depends on GC write amplification (WAF) and per-node walk cost, not a certainty.
3. Before GC, at about 64K IOPS with bs=4K, NAND lpn capacity for MAP=8K/16K/32K (about 286K/143K/71K lpn/s) already exceeds demand. Correct accounting would not throttle those cases either. Before GC, the hidden penalty mainly affects MAP=64K/128K. After GC starts it affects every bs<MAP pair.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The core claim is correct. For the 15 pairs with bs<MAP, conv_write takes bs bytes from the shared write buffer but releases MAP bytes per programmed lpn when NAND completes. buffer_release has no cap, so remaining climbs past buf->size and the remaining<size check effectively never fires again. It could only fire if the host byte rate exceeded programs/s x ONESHOT, roughly 2.3 to 6.2 GB/s. With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1, host completion time is firmware plus PCIe only, so NAND and GC backlog no longer throttle the host in the timing model. When NAND demand exceeds capacity, lun->next_lun_avail_time drifts further ahead. This always happens after GC starts, and before GC for MAP=64K/128K at about 64K IOPS. Two failures follow.
(a) Once more than 16384 pending release ops pile up on one worker (IO_WORKER_BY_SQ), __enqueue_io_req silently drops host commands. The SQ entry is consumed and never completed.
(b) Beyond 393 ms of drift, chmodel_request logs "Need to increase array size" and charges zero channel time.

Refinements:
- The growing backlog does reach host IOPS through one indirect path. __insert_req_sorted walks O(pending future-dated ops) for every host completion, so dispatcher CPU cost rises with the backlog. This is an emulator artifact, not modeled NAND time, and it may hold the backlog below 16384, so (a) is likely rather than certain.
- Before GC, for MAP=8K/16K/32K with bs=4K, NAND is not the bottleneck anyway. There the hidden penalty shows up mainly after GC starts.
- The proposed dmesg screen cannot find "IO queue is almost full". WARN_ON_ONCE("...") uses the string as its condition and prints "WARNING: ... io.c:302 __allocate_work_queue_entry" once per module load. Grep for "__allocate_work_queue_entry" or "WARNING:", plus "Need to increase array size" and "No free line left".
- The suggested fix is sound: allocate (end_lpn-start_lpn+1)*pgsz and return false on shortfall. That amount is at most 128K, below WB, which is 1 to 4 MiB. Running only bs>=MAP also avoids the problem.

verdicts.reasoning:
The central mechanism checks out in the code. The two failure modes and the detection advice are partly wrong.

**What the code confirms (MAP=128K, bs=4K)**
- In this configuration FLASH = ONESHOT = 128K, pgs_per_oneshotpg = 1 and GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*128K*2 = 4 MiB.
- Each request calls buffer_allocate(4096) (conv_ftl.c:961). Every lpn is last_pg_in_wordline, so each request issues one 128K program and calls schedule_internal_operation(..., 1*131072) (conv_ftl.c:1001-1008). The net gain per request is +126,976 B.
- In general the code takes bs bytes and gives back ONESHOT bytes per pgs_per_oneshotpg lpns, which averages MAP bytes per lpn. It is symmetric only when bs >= MAP. There are 15 of 36 pairs with bs < MAP: correct.
- buffer.remaining is a size_t with no cap (ssd.c:39-47). buffer_refill is only called from zns_mgmt_send.c, never from the conv FTL.
- A worked example: remaining = 4M - N*4K + P*128K stays above 4K unless almost no programs ever complete, so the check never fails again within a 60 s run.
- WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 makes the target time nsecs_xfer_completed: start + 4000 + 460 ns per 4K + PCIe (ssd.c:349-360). GC writes take no buffer and enqueue no release ops (gc_write_page). So modelled NAND and GC time never reaches the host for bs < MAP.
- The capacity numbers are correct. xfer_lat is 152 ns per 128 B, so a 128K transfer is 155,648 ns; plus tPROG 185,000 ns over 16 LUNs gives 46,970/s. The same method gives 60,878/s (64K) and 71,457/s (32K).
- The (a) code path is real. CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ is defined (nvmev.h:12), and the smoke run's dmesg shows "1/0/0 default/read/poll queues", i.e. one SQ, so everything lands on one worker. A full queue gives a NULL from io.c:301-303 and a silent drop at io.c:325-327.
- The (b) code path is also real (channel_model.c:73-76, 98304 x 4 us = 393 ms).

**Where the claim is wrong or overstated**
1. "NAND time no longer reaches the host at all" is only true for modelled latency. Backlog leaks back as CPU cost:
   - __insert_req_sorted (io.c:250-292) walks backward from the tail past every pending internal op, so each host insert costs O(pending).
   - The worker loop (io.c:624-695) scans the whole list.
   - The existing smoke run results/pre_smoke_test/base/map128k_bs4k_r1 (WBUF_FIX=0) shows this. IOPS was 56K in the first 0.5 s, then held at about 47K (≈46,970, the NAND capacity) before GC, then fell from 23K to 16K after GC.
   - So IOPS tracks the NAND backlog through simulator overhead rather than through the model. The data is still invalid, but not for the reason stated.
2. Failure (a) is stated as a certain result with a 0.35 s threshold, but that ignores two limiters:
   - The O(pending) slowdown above holds pre-GC IOPS near capacity.
   - The 393 ms clamp in (b) returns zero channel time. Beyond 393 ms of backlog the LUN cycle falls to 185 us (about 86.5K programs/s before GC), so the backlog tends to hover near 393 ms. Pending ops ≈ 0.393 s x user-program completion rate, which passes 16384 only if completions exceed about 41.7K/s.
   - In the actual 10 s worst-case run, fio reported error=0 with 260,141 I/Os and clat max 5.4 ms; it finished at 10.3 s with no timeout.
   - So command drops and hangs are possible but not shown. They should not be stated as a consequence that follows.
3. Failure (b) is confirmed and worse than claimed. That run produced 1,859,673 '[chmodel_request]' errors in 10 s, both 'Need to increase array size' and 'No free entry'. These are unthrottled printk calls from the dispatcher. They eat dispatcher CPU and overflowed the kernel log buffer ('Dropped 93506 similar message(s)'), which can hide other messages.
4. The detection advice is wrong. WARN_ON_ONCE("IO queue is almost full") (io.c:302) never prints that string; the kernel only prints 'WARNING: ... at .../io.c:302 __allocate_work_queue_entry'.
5. Minor: remaining passes buf->size after the first completed oneshot program, not "a few hundred requests". In principle the buffer would engage again if D*bs > C*MAP once the surplus runs out, but the gigabytes of surplus built up before GC rule that out within 60 s.

**The suggested fix is sound**
- need = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * pgsz is at most 128K, and WB is 1-4 MiB, so the assert at ssd.c:23 still holds.
- The release side is pgsz per lpn, so allocation and release become symmetric.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The blocker stands, but its failure modes and detection advice need correcting.

**Confirmed:** for every bs < MAP pair (15 of 36), conv_write takes only the bytes the host sent from the write buffer (conv_ftl.c:961). It gives back one full oneshot page per program (conv_ftl.c:1007-1008), which averages MAP bytes per lpn. remaining has no upper limit (ssd.c:43), and conv never calls buffer_refill. Example for MAP=128K, bs=4K: each request takes 4,096 B and later returns 131,072 B, a net gain of +126,976 B, with a 4 MiB buffer. The buffer stops throttling as soon as the first program completes and never throttles again within a 60 s run. With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 the host completion time is firmware + PCIe only, and GC writes bypass the buffer entirely. Modelled NAND and GC time therefore never reaches host latency, so bs < MAP results do not measure program or GC cost and are invalid unless fixed.

**Corrections:**
1. The NAND backlog does affect host IOPS, but only through simulator CPU overhead, not through modelled time. The sorted insert is O(pending) (io.c:265-273) and the worker scans the whole list. In the existing 10 s run for MAP=128K, bs=4K, IOPS levelled off at about 47K (≈ the 46,970 programs/s NAND capacity) before GC, then dropped from 23K to 16K after GC.
2. The 393 ms channel-model overflow is confirmed and severe. It logged 1.86M '[chmodel_request]' messages in 10 s ('Need to increase array size' and 'No free entry'), returned zero channel time, flooded the dispatcher with printk, and overran the kernel log buffer.
3. Overflowing the 16384-entry work queue and silently dropping commands (io.c:301-303, 325-327; one SQ, so one worker) is a real code path but is not a proven outcome. The 393 ms clamp and the O(pending) slowdown limit how far the backlog grows. Pending ops are roughly 0.393 s x completion rate, which passes 16384 only above about 41.7K completions/s. The 10 s worst-case run finished cleanly: fio error 0, clat max 5.4 ms.

**Fix:** charge need = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * spp->pgsz in conv_write (at most 128K, below the 1-4 MiB buffer, so the assert at ssd.c:23 holds). Optionally also cap remaining in buffer_release. Alternatively, run only pairs with bs >= MAP.

**Detection:** do not grep for 'IO queue is almost full'; WARN_ON_ONCE never prints that string. Instead reject a run if any of these appear:
- 'WARNING:' together with 'io.c:302' or '__allocate_work_queue_entry'
- '[chmodel_request]'
- 'No free line left in VIRT'
- nvme timeout, abort or reset messages
- a nonzero fio error

Count messages from a live 'dmesg -W' stream, because the overrun buffer drops messages.

verified.title: Making FLASH_PAGE_SIZE 64K/128K while tPROG/tR stay fixed raises NAND bandwidth 1.7x / 2.6x (confound between MAP<=32K and MAP 64K/128K)
verified.affects: Any comparison between MAP in {4K..32K} (FLASH 32K) and MAP in {64K, 128K} (FLASH = MAP). Strongest at large bs and after GC starts.
verified.evidence: A NAND write is one channel transfer of the whole oneshot page followed by a fixed tPROG: chmodel_request(ch, chnl_stime, ncmd->xfer_size), then nand_etime = nand_stime + spp->pg_wr_lat (ssd.c:420-431). xfer_size = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT (conv_ftl.c:951). pg_wr_lat = NAND_PROG_LATENCY = 185000 ns for every page size (ssd_config.h:95; ssd.c:117). Channel cost is 152 ns per 128 B (channel_model.h:40, BANDWIDTH_TO_TX_TIME(800)). Per-die cycle: 32K = 38,912+185,000 = 223,912 ns, i.e. 139.6 MiB/s. 64K = 262,824 ns, i.e. 237.8 MiB/s. 128K = 340,648 ns, i.e. 366.9 MiB/s. Across 16 dies the ceilings are 2,233 / 3,805 / 5,871 MiB/s. The host write path also passes the shared PCIe model at 3360 (ssd.c:349-360; conv_ftl.c:397-405), about 3,357 MiB/s. So MAP<=32K is NAND-bound at about 2.23 GiB/s while MAP 64K/128K is PCIe-bound at about 3.3 GiB/s. GC reads are affected the same way: tR is fixed (NAND_READ_LATENCY ~30/42 us at ssd_config.h:92-93, chosen at ssd.c:394-398), so each 64K/128K flash-page read moves 2x/4x more data for the same sensing time.
verified.impact_on_results: Higher bandwidth or smaller GC slowdown at MAP 64K/128K can come from the bigger NAND page, not from the mapping unit. The step between MAP=32K and MAP=64K cannot be attributed to MAP.
verified.suggested_fix: Option 1: keep bandwidth per byte constant by scaling the latencies with FLASH/32K. NAND_PROG_LATENCY becomes 370000 (64K) and 740000 (128K), which reproduces 139.6 MiB/s per die exactly because the transfer scales linearly too: 65536/(77,824+370,000) = 32768/223,912. Scale NAND_READ_LATENCY_* by the same factor. Option 2: use one NAND geometry for all six MAPs, e.g. FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=KB(128), which satisfies the ssd.c:98 assert for every MAP <= 128K. Either way, state the choice in the document.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the code path line by line, and every step the auditor cites is correct.

1) Write timing per die. ssd_advance_nand NAND_WRITE (ssd.c:420-431) sets chnl_stime = max(lun->next_lun_avail_time, cmd_stime) and calls chmodel_request(ch, chnl_stime, ncmd->xfer_size). It then sets nand_etime = chnl_etime + spp->pg_wr_lat and lun->next_lun_avail_time = nand_etime. A die therefore runs the channel transfer and then tPROG one after the other, with no overlap.
- Host writes: xfer_size = pgsz * pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE (conv_ftl.c:951).
- GC writes use the same size (conv_ftl.c:627).

- 32K: 256 units, 38,912 ns. 64K: 77,824 ns. 128K: 155,648 ns.

- Per-die cycle and bandwidth: 223,912 ns = 139.6 MiB/s (32K); 262,824 ns = 237.8 MiB/s (64K); 340,648 ns = 366.9 MiB/s (128K).

5) PCIe bound. The PCIe model is shared (conv_ftl.c:397-405) and charged in ssd_advance_write_buffer (ssd.c:349-360). Credits are MB(3360)*4000/1e9/128 = 110 per 4 us, which is about 3357 MiB/s. 7) Proposed fix. The arithmetic checks out: 65536/(77,824+370,000) = 32768/223,912, because both numerator and denominator double. FLASH_PAGE_SIZE = KB(128) satisfies the ssd.c:98 asserts for every power-of-two MAP <= 128K.

GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = NAND_CHANNELS * LUNS_PER_NAND_CH * ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE * 2 (ssd_config.h:105) also grows with FLASH_PAGE_SIZE: 1 MiB at 32K, 2 MiB at 64K, 4 MiB at 128K. Option 1 (scaling the latencies) does not equalize this buffer. Pinning GLOBAL_WB_SIZE, or Option 2 (one geometry for all MAPs), does.

A practical note: at bs=4K the measured ~250 MiB/s is far below either ceiling, so the confound matters mainly at large bs and after GC starts, which matches what the claim says.

- pgs_per_oneshotpg = 1, so every IO programs.

- Starting from 2 MiB, `remaining` keeps growing past `size`, so buffer_allocate never fails and the buffer never throttles writes.

Example 2, MAP=8K and bs=4K:
- Each partition programs after 4 lpns, which is 4 IOs and 16 KiB allocated.
- That program releases 32 KiB, so `remaining` also inflates (2x over-release).

- One IO is 32 lpns, which is 8 per partition and fills one wordline in each.

verified.title: Sub-page writes are not modelled as read-modify-write

verified.evidence: For each lpn, conv_write only invalidates the old PPA, takes a new page and updates the map (conv_ftl.c:971-998). verified.impact_on_results: The sub-page penalty consists only of program amplification (MAP/bs NAND bytes per host byte) plus earlier GC. The tR + transfer of a real RMW is missing, so the penalty for small bs at large MAP is underestimated (in addition to C1).

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the write path in upstream 61c90f7 and the code supports the claim.

1) conv_write (conv_ftl.c:925 onward) computes start_lpn and end_lpn as lba / secs_per_pg. The per-lpn loop runs from line 971. For each lpn it calls get_maptbl_ent. If the lpn is already mapped (line 980), it only runs mark_page_invalid and set_rmap_ent(INVALID_LPN). It then calls get_new_page, set_maptbl_ent, set_rmap_ent, mark_page_valid and advance_write_pointer (line 998). Once the last page in a wordline is reached, it issues one NAND_WRITE with xfer = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg (line 1004). conv_write never builds a NAND_READ command. In conv_ftl.c, NAND_READ appears only in gc_read_page (around lines 587 and 720, both GC_IO) and in conv_read (line 854). Nothing checks whether the write covers only part of the lpn. A partly covered, already-mapped lpn is handled exactly like a full overwrite, so a read-modify-write (RMW) costs no tR and no channel transfer.

2) Data stays correct because io.c:109 runs memcpy(ns.mapped + offset, ...), where offset = slba << LBA_BITS (__cmd_io_offset, io.c:39-42). Data is stored by byte address and is independent of the FTL mapping. The claim cites io.c:107-109 correctly.

3) The amplification claim also holds. Each write with bs < MAP consumes a full pgsz = MAP slot of the oneshot page. The NAND program and GC (through consume_write_credit per lpn) therefore see MAP/bs bytes per host byte.

Refinement (this does not refute the claim, but it adds to the impact and affects the suggested fix): With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION = 1 (970PRO bundle), the host's completion time is nsecs_xfer_completed, which is the write-buffer and PCIe time from ssd_advance_write_buffer. NAND time reaches host latency only through write-buffer back-pressure. buffer_allocate takes LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba), the host bytes (bs). Each oneshot page then releases pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz bytes (schedule_internal_operation at conv_ftl.c:1007, buffer_release at io.c:671). When bs < MAP, release exceeds allocation by a factor of MAP/bs, so buf->remaining grows past the buffer size and back-pressure is effectively lost. This means even the program amplification and GC penalty may not show up in host IOPS and latency for bs < MAP. The suggested fix (a NAND_READ before the program, using its completion as swr.stime) would only delay buffer release. Because release is already over-credited, the fix would have little visible effect unless the buffer accounting is also corrected (for example, allocating MAP-rounded bytes per lpn) or the RMW read is placed on the host completion path.

For bs < MAP it is 12,160 x bs/MAP MiB, e.g. 380 MiB for MAP=128K bs=4K. Also, fio's default random map (norandommap=0) writes every block exactly once per pass. So for bs >= MAP no page is invalid until 11,483 MiB have been written, and at GC onset the victim lines are still about 94% valid (677/11,483 invalidated), which gives a sharp cliff. randrepeat=1 (the default) makes all 3 repetitions use the same LBA sequence.

verified.suggested_fix: Add write_bw_log/write_iops_log/write_lat_log with log_avg_msec=1000, and report the pre-GC and post-GC phases separately (the onset is visible in the 1-s log).
