verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the code at commit 61c90f7 and it supports the claim.

Capacity: main.c:498 sets storage_size = 12 GiB - 1 MiB = 12,883,853,312 B. conv_init_namespace splits this into SSD_PARTITIONS=4, so each partition has 2 channels x 2 LUNs. ssd.c sets blk_size = DIV_ROUND_UP(3,220,963,328, 384*1*2*2) = 2,096,982 B. That rounds up to 64x32K, 32x64K or 16x128K oneshot pages, so the block is exactly 2 MiB for every MAP, including the MAP=64K/128K cases with FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=MAP. blks_per_line = tt_luns = 4, so a line is 8 MiB, and tt_lines = blks_per_lun = 384. ns->size = size*100/107 = 12,040,984,403 B = 11,483.2 MiB.

Init: init_lines puts all 384 lines on the free list. prepare_write_pointer for USER_IO and GC_IO (conv_ftl.c:349-350) each take one line, which leaves free_line_cnt = 382.

Trigger: init_write_flow_control sets both write_credits and credits_to_refill to pgs_per_line. In conv_write, advance_write_pointer runs before consume_write_credit and check_and_refill_write_credit (lines 1011-1012). So the credit reaches 0 on exactly the page that completes a line, and that is when free_line_cnt drops to 382-k. foreground_gc (815-822) calls do_gc only when free_line_cnt <= gc_thres_lines_high = 2 (line 371). That first happens at k = 380 lines per partition, i.e. 380 x 8 MiB x 4 = 12,160 MiB of page writes, which is 1.0589x the exported size. Nothing else calls do_gc: should_gc() is unused and there is no background GC.

Page writes per host write: conv_write allocates one new full page for every LPN in [start_lpn, end_lpn], with no read-modify-write. So for bs >= MAP (aligned powers of two), page bytes equal host bytes. For bs < MAP, each IO writes one MAP-sized page, which gives 12,160 x bs/MAP MiB of host writes (380 MiB for MAP=128K, bs=4K).

Victims: with fio's default random map, each block is written once per pass, and time_based resets the map each loop. So for bs >= MAP, mark_page_invalid is first called only after 11,483 MiB. Until then every line goes to full_line_list. At onset about 677 MiB, or 5.9%, has been invalidated. do_gc(force=true) takes the minimum-vpc line from the pqueue, which is a min-heap because cmppri is next > curr. It copies the remaining ~94% valid pages and sets credits_to_refill = victim->ipc, which is small. That makes a sharp write-amplification cliff.

fio 3.36 defaults to randrepeat=1, so all repetitions use the same offset sequence.

Minor quantitative nuances, none of which change the conclusion:
(a) "About 94% valid" is the average over first-pass lines. The chosen victim is the minimum-vpc line, so it is somewhat less valid: roughly 92-93% at MAP=4K, and noticeably lower at MAP=128K, where a line has only 64 pages and the variance is larger.
(b) The 48.6 s figure assumes the pre-GC rate is the measured 250 MiB/s. If that 250 MiB/s is a 60-s mean that already includes the GC phase, the pre-GC rate was higher and onset came earlier.
(c) The 2,233 and 3,357 MiB/s values are illustrative throughputs, not quantities derived from the code.
(d) The checks happen every pgs_per_line pages only until the first GC. After that the interval becomes victim->ipc.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The claim is essentially correct. Each partition has 384 lines of 8 MiB (4 LUNs x 2 MiB blocks), and 2 of them are taken by the user and GC write pointers at init, leaving 382 free. foreground_gc is checked whenever a partition's write credit reaches zero, which before the first GC is every pgs_per_line user pages (one full line). It fires only when free_line_cnt <= 2. So the first GC happens after 380 lines per partition, i.e. 12,160 MiB of page writes, about 1.059x the exported 11,483 MiB. For bs >= MAP that is 12,160 MiB of host writes. For bs < MAP it is 12,160 x bs/MAP MiB, because conv_write programs a whole MAP-sized page for each sub-page write.

With fio's default random map, the first pass invalidates nothing when bs >= MAP. At onset only about 5.9% of first-pass data is invalid, so on average lines are about 94% valid. The minimum-vpc victim that GC picks is somewhat less valid than that average (lower still at MAP=128K, where a line has only 64 pages), but GC still causes a sharp throughput cliff.

The onset time inside the 60-s window therefore depends on MAP, bs and the pre-GC throughput. The 48.6 s figure is an upper estimate if 250 MiB/s is a 60-s mean that already includes GC. With ramp_time=0, the 60-s mean mixes the pre-GC (FOB) and GC regimes in proportions that differ per configuration. With randrepeat=1 (the default), all 3 repetitions use the same LBA sequence, so they measure emulator timing noise rather than workload variation.

Logging per-second bandwidth/IOPS/latency (log_avg_msec=1000) and reporting the two phases separately is a sound fix.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the claim against the code (upstream 61c90f7, read-only) and against the first-GC dmesg lines from runs already on this server (exp/results/main_20261008/base and pre_smoke_test). Both agree with the claim.

Geometry. main.c:498 sets storage_size = 12 GiB - 1 MiB = 12,883,853,312 B, so each of the 4 partitions gets 3,220,963,328 B. ssd.c computes blk_size = DIV_ROUND_UP(cap, 384*1*2*2) = 2,096,982 B. That rounds up to 64 oneshot pages of 32 KiB for MAP<=32K, 32 x 64K for MAP=64K, and 16 x 128K for MAP=128K. A block is therefore exactly 2 MiB and a line (4 LUNs per partition) is 8 MiB for every MAP. tt_lines = blks_per_lun = 384.

GC onset. conv_ftl.c:349-350 takes 2 lines at init, so 382 lines are free. advance_write_pointer takes a new line every time a user line fills. init_write_flow_control gives write_credits = pgs_per_line, and check_and_refill_write_credit (100-108, called at 1012) calls foreground_gc when credits reach 0. That happens exactly at a line boundary. foreground_gc runs do_gc only if free_line_cnt <= gc_thres_lines_high = 2 (line 371, lines 21-24, 815-822). should_gc / gc_thres_lines is never called, so there is no other GC path. The first GC therefore comes after 380 full lines per partition: 380 x 8 MiB x 4 = 12,160 MiB of page writes. ns->size = storage*100/107 gives 11,483.18 MiB exported, so the ratio is 1.0589.

Empirical check. dmesg shows host_pgs = 778,240 (= 380 x 2048) per partition at first GC for MAP=4K with bs=4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K and 128K. It shows 389,120 (= 380 x 1024) for MAP=8K bs=4K and 24,320 (= 380 x 64) for MAP=128K bs=4K. All three match the formula.

bs vs MAP. In conv_write, a bs-aligned write with bs < MAP has start_lpn == end_lpn, so it programs one full MAP page. Onset in host bytes is then 12,160 x bs/MAP MiB:
- MAP=128K, bs=4K: 24,320 x 4 x 4 KiB = 380 MiB. Correct.
- MAP=8K, bs=4K: 6,080 MiB.

The bandwidth logs confirm the timing:
- MAP=4K, bs=32K and bs=128K run at 2,233 MiB/s and cliff at about 5.5-6.0 s, at roughly 12.2 GB cumulative.
- MAP=4K, bs=4K runs at about 2,000 MiB/s and cliffs at about 6.2 s.

fio side. job.fio sets randrepeat=1 explicitly. norandommap defaults to 0, so each block is written once per pass, and with bs >= MAP no LPN is invalidated before 11,483 MiB. In the bs32k and bs128k runs, all 4 partitions pick the same victim line with the same vpc. That is consistent with an identical, deterministic LBA sequence, so the repetitions vary only in emulator timing.

Minor inaccuracies, not enough to refute:
(a) "victims ~94% valid" is the average line, 677/11,483 = 5.9% invalid. GC picks the line with the lowest vpc, and the real first victims for bs >= MAP have vpc 1848-1902 of 2048, i.e. 90-93% valid. The cliff is still sharp.
(b) The "48.6 s at the measured 250 MiB/s" example is right arithmetic, but 250 MiB/s is a GC-diluted mean. The pre-GC rate at MAP=4K bs=4K is about 2,000 MiB/s, so onset there is about 6 s, not 48.6 s.
(c) The claim leaves out a further effect of norandommap=0. When fio's second pass nears completion (about 2 x 11,483 MiB cumulative), victims are almost fully invalid and throughput recovers to 1.4-1.9 GB/s. A third pass then starts and throughput collapses again (visible at t≈36-38 s for bs32k/bs128k and t≈51 s for bs4k). The 60-s window can therefore contain FOB, GC, recovery and a second cliff, which makes the means even less comparable.
(d) For bs < MAP the victims are mostly invalid at onset: vpc 12-18 of 64 for MAP=128K bs=4K, and 375 of 1024 for MAP=8K bs=4K. In those runs the post-GC drop is milder and has a different shape from the bs >= MAP cliff.
(e) The suggested logging fix is already in the job file (write_bw/iops/lat_log with log_avg_msec=500).
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The claim is essentially correct.

Per partition there are 384 lines of 4 x 2 MiB = 8 MiB. This holds for every MAP: blk_size = ceil(3,220,963,328 / 1536) = 2,096,982 B, which rounds to exactly 2 MiB of oneshot pages. Two lines are reserved at init. Foreground GC runs only when free_line_cnt <= 2, so the first GC fires after 380 x 8 MiB x 4 = 12,160 MiB of page writes, which is 1.059x the exported 11,483 MiB. In host bytes that is 12,160 MiB for bs >= MAP and 12,160 x bs/MAP for bs < MAP (380 MiB at MAP=128K bs=4K). dmesg confirms it: host_pgs at first GC = 778,240 (MAP=4K), 389,120 (MAP=8K bs=4K) and 24,320 (MAP=128K bs=4K) per partition.

Corrections to the details:
- **Victim validity:** for bs >= MAP the first victim is the line with the lowest vpc, about 90-93% valid (vpc 1848-1902 of 2048), not 94%. 94% is the average line.
- **Onset time at MAP=4K bs=4K:** the pre-GC rate there is about 2,000 MiB/s, so GC starts at about 6 s. The 250 MiB/s figure is a GC-diluted mean, so the 48.6 s example does not apply.
- **Second cliff (norandommap=0):** throughput also recovers near the end of each full fio pass (about 23 GB cumulative) and collapses again when the next pass starts. Some 60-s windows therefore contain FOB, GC, recovery and a second cliff in config-dependent proportions.
- **bs < MAP:** victims are mostly invalid at onset (19-37% valid), so the drop is milder.

randrepeat=1 does give an identical LBA sequence in all 3 repetitions, so the repetitions capture only emulator timing noise. The per-phase reporting from the bandwidth/IOPS/latency logs (already enabled with log_avg_msec=500) is the right fix.

audit.computed_geometry:
All values below come from upstream 61c90f7 code with the planned edits (secs_per_pg = MAP/512; BLKS_PER_PLN = 384; FLASH = ONESHOT = 32K for MAP<=32K and = MAP for 64K/128K; insmod memmap_size=12G).
Capacity input: storage_size = 12GiB - 1MiB = 12,883,853,312 B (main.c:497-498). It is split into 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:386, ssd.c:82-84), so each partition gets 3,220,963,328 B, nchs = 2, luns_per_ch = 2, tt_luns = 4, blks_per_pl = 384 = tt_lines (ssd.c:155-158).
blk_size = DIV_ROUND_UP(cap, 384*1*2*2) = 2,096,982 B (ssd.c:89). oneshotpgs_per_blk = ceil(blk_size/ONESHOT) = 64 (MAP<=32K), 32 (64K), 16 (128K) (ssd.c:102). Every effective block is therefore exactly 2 MiB and every line (4 blocks) is 8 MiB.

Per MAP (4K/8K/16K/32K/64K/128K):
- pgs_per_oneshotpg = pgs_per_flashpg: 8/4/2/1/1/1
- pgs_per_blk: 512/256/128/64/32/16
- pgs_per_line: 2048/1024/512/256/128/64
- tt_pgs per partition: 786,432/393,216/196,608/98,304/49,152/24,576 (x4 for the device)
- Physical size: 4 x 384 x 8 MiB = 12 GiB for every MAP. This is 1 MiB more than the backing store, which does not matter because the backing store only holds logical data.

Exported capacity: pba_pcent = (int)(1.07*100) = 107 (conv_ftl.c:373). ns->size = 12,883,853,312*100/107 = 12,040,984,403 B (conv_ftl.c:411). nsze = 23,517,547 LBAs of 512 B = 12,040,984,064 B = 11.214 GiB (admin.c:315). OP = 7.0% of logical. Per partition the LPN space fills 358.85 lines out of 384, leaving 25.15 spare lines.

GC onset: GC starts when free_line_cnt <= 2 (conv_ftl.c:21-24, 370-371). There are 384 lines minus 2 open lines (user and GC write pointers, conv_ftl.c:349-350), so the threshold is reached once 380 lines per partition have been user-written. That is 380 x 4 x 8 MiB = 12,160 MiB of user page-writes, the same for every MAP. In page-writes (= host writes when bs<=MAP) this is 3,112,960 / 1,556,480 / 778,240 / 389,120 / 194,560 / 97,280. A timing-free re-implementation of the conv_ftl bookkeeping reproduces these exactly (scratchpad/wasim.py: onset at host write 3,113,932 / 1,557,062 / 778,368 / 388,295 / 195,117 / 97,826 for bs=4K).

Seconds to GC onset:
- bs<=MAP at about 64K IOPS (250 MiB/s at 4K): 48.6 / 24.3 / 12.2 / 6.1 / 3.0 / 1.5 s.
- bs>=MAP: t = 12,160 MiB / host_MiB_per_s. Examples: 48.6 s at 250 MiB/s, 12.2 s at 1 GiB/s, 6.1 s at 2 GiB/s. No GC happens at all in 60 s below 202.7 MiB/s.

Write buffer: GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*ONESHOT*2 = 1/1/1/1/2/4 MiB (ssd_config.h:105), shared by the 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:397-405).

Mapping metadata (vmalloc): maptbl = 8 B x tt_pgs x 4 = 24/12/6/3/1.5/0.75 MiB, and rmap is the same size (conv_ftl.c:305, 321), so maptbl+rmap = 48/24/12/6/3/1.5 MiB. nand_page metadata is 16 B per page plus kmalloc(4*secs_per_pg) (ssd.c:174-183), about 144/120/108/102/99/97.5 MiB.

Timing constants:
- NAND channel: 152 ns per 128 B; 26 credits per 4 us, about 793 MiB/s.
- PCIe: 36 ns per 128 B; 110 credits per 4 us, about 3.36 GiB/s (channel_model.h:40-42).
- Program cycle per LUN = xfer(ONESHOT) + 185 us: 223.9 / 223.9 / 223.9 / 223.9 / 262.8 / 340.6 us. Peak program bandwidth over 16 LUNs is 2233 MiB/s (MAP<=32K), 3805 MiB/s (64K) and 5871 MiB/s (128K). In programs per second that is 71,457 / 60,877 / 46,969.
- Channel model horizon: 98,304 x 4 us = 393 ms (channel_model.h:127-128).
- Host-visible write latency (early completion) is 4000 + 460*ceil(bs/4K) + PCIe: 5,612 ns at bs=4K and 55,584 ns at bs=128K.

Write amplification from the simulation (greedy GC, fio randommap permutation per pass):
- Steady state: about 8.1-8.6 for every MAP.
- bs>=MAP: WA is 1.0 until 12,160 MiB, jumps to about 7-9 right after onset, decays during pass 2 (down to about 1.5), then spikes again at pass 3. MAP=4K/bs=4K: about 8.8 / 7.5 / 7.3 / 6.8 in the 160K-write windows after onset.
- bs<MAP: WA rises gradually after onset. MAP=128K/bs=4K reaches 7.6 by about 2.3 GiB of host data; 32K/4K reaches about 8.3 by about 6.9 GiB; 8K/4K reaches about 8.6 by about 11.9 GiB.

all_claims.title: Write-buffer over-release when bs < MAP removes all NAND/GC back-pressure on the host
all_claims.affects: All 15 bs<MAP combos: MAP=8K bs=4K; 16K bs=4,8K; 32K bs=4,8,16K; 64K bs=4..32K; 128K bs=4..64K
all_claims.evidence: Allocation uses host bytes: conv_ftl.c:961 'buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba))'. Release uses full mapping units: every time a oneshot page completes, conv_ftl.c:1001-1008 calls 'schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz)', and that release happens at NAND completion (io.c:668-673). For aligned bs<MAP each host write is exactly 1 LPN, i.e. one MAP page (conv_ftl.c:937-938). So one oneshot page = pgs_per_oneshotpg writes allocating pgs_per_oneshotpg*bs bytes, but ONESHOT bytes are released. Net gain per oneshot is ONESHOT*(1-bs/MAP): +16K per 4 writes at MAP=8K/bs=4K, +124K per write at MAP=128K/bs=4K. buffer_release just adds with no clamp (ssd.c:39-46), and the only place the host is throttled is buffer_allocate returning 0 when remaining<size (ssd.c:29-31 -> conv_ftl.c:962-963 -> io.c:474-475, 525-526). Completion time itself is NAND-independent under WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1: ret->nsecs_target = nsecs_xfer_completed, i.e. the fw+PCIe time from ssd.c:349-360 (conv_ftl.c:965-967, 1015-1021). At 64K IOPS 'remaining' grows by roughly 0.25-7.6 GiB/s, so after the first few ms the buffer never blocks.
all_claims.impact_on_results: For bs<MAP the measured IOPS/BW reflects only the emulator's dispatcher CPU path. NAND program amplification (MAP bytes programmed per bs-byte write) and the whole GC cost are invisible to fio. MAP=128K/bs=4K would therefore show roughly the same ~64K IOPS as MAP=4K/bs=4K, even though NAND demand is 32x higher and GC starts at 1.5 s. With correct coupling, NAND capacity would be about 47K IOPS before GC and about 4.2K IOPS (~16 MiB/s) at the steady GC WA of 7.6. Any paper conclusion about small writes under coarse mapping drawn from these points would be wrong.
all_claims.suggested_fix: In the experiment copy, buffer whole mapping units so that allocation equals release: replace conv_ftl.c:961-963 with 'size_t wb = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * spp->pgsz; allocated_buf_size = buffer_allocate(wbuf, wb); if (allocated_buf_size < wb) return false;'. This is unchanged for bs>=MAP (aligned) and satisfies the assert at ssd.c:23, since WB (1/2/4 MiB) >= MAP. Otherwise, drop bs<MAP from the matrix or report it as invalid.

all_claims.title: Consequence of C1: unbounded NAND backlog leads to work-queue exhaustion, dropped completions, O(n) emulator slowdowns and unratelimited printk floods
all_claims.affects: bs<MAP combos; worst for MAP>=32K (one internal op per host write), then 16K and 8K
all_claims.evidence: Every completed oneshot enqueues an internal buffer-release entry whose target is the NAND completion time (io.c:357-388). Each worker has NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO=16384 entries (nvmev.h:58), and there are 2 workers with cpus=3,4,5. When the free list runs out, __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-304). __enqueue_io_req then silently returns (io.c:325-327) after the SQ entry has already been consumed (io.c:528-533), so the NVMe command never gets a CQE. Sorted insertion walks back over every far-future entry (io.c:264-274), and the worker loop traverses the whole list on every pass (io.c:624-695), so dispatcher and worker CPU cost grow O(pending). Once the LUN backlog exceeds 98,304 x 4 us = 393 ms (channel_model.h:127-128), chmodel_request prints NVMEV_ERROR 'Need to increase array size' and returns request_time with zero transfer time (channel_model.c:73-77). NVMEV_ERROR is a plain printk(KERN_ERR) (nvmev.h:41). Estimate for MAP=128K/bs=4K: host demand of 64K programs/s exceeds the 46,969/s capacity before GC, so the backlog reaches the 393 ms horizon after about 1 s and pending internal ops sit around 25K out of the ~32.7K total. After GC onset (1.5 s), capacity with tPROG only falls to 9.7-40K/s, so pending entries grow by tens of thousands per second and overflow within seconds. Same mechanism for MAP=32K/bs=4K after about 7-10 s and 16K/bs=4K after about 20-25 s. These times are estimates; the mechanism is directly in the code.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Expected outcomes are hung I/O and nvme timeouts/resets, or IOPS collapses caused by emulator list-walk and printk overhead rather than by the SSD model. Either way the run is invalid.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Fix C1. After every run, also save dmesg and grep for 'IO queue is almost full', 'Need to increase array size', 'No free entry' and 'nvme.*timeout'. Discard any run that shows them.

all_claims.title: Partial writes (bs<MAP): no read-modify-write read is modeled; data integrity is preserved by the flat logical backing store
all_claims.affects: All bs<MAP combos (the performance model only)
all_claims.evidence: conv_write issues only invalidate + allocate + program (conv_ftl.c:971-1013). The old MAP page is marked invalid wholesale (conv_ftl.c:980-985) and no NAND_READ of the old ppa is ever issued. The program does charge a full MAP unit per write: swr.xfer_size = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg (conv_ftl.c:951) and every lpn consumes one pgsz page. Data is never handled by the FTL: there is no memcpy in conv_ftl.c or ssd.c (grep), gc_write_page says 'move valid page data (already in DRAM)' (conv_ftl.c:597), and the io worker copies to ns->mapped + (slba<<LBA_BITS) (io.c:39-42, 107-111) or to the DMA target storage_start+offset (io.c:236). The bytes in the rest of the mapping unit therefore stay intact and readable.
all_claims.impact_on_results: No data is silently dropped. Timing still underestimates the cost of a partial write: the RMW read (one tR of about 36 us plus a MAP-sized channel transfer, e.g. 38.9 us at 32K) is missing for every bs<MAP write to an already mapped LPN. Program-side amplification (MAP/bs) is modeled, but only becomes visible once C1 is fixed.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Optional: in conv_write, if (nr_lba*512 < pgsz) and the old ppa is mapped, issue a NAND_READ of the old ppa (xfer=pgsz) before the program and set the program stime to at least that read's completion. Otherwise state in the paper that the RMW read is not modeled.

all_claims.title: FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=MAP for 64K/128K changes the simulated NAND hardware and confounds the MAP comparison
all_claims.affects: MAP=64K and MAP=128K (all bs) compared against MAP<=32K
all_claims.evidence: tPROG is charged once per program regardless of size (ssd.c:427-428, NAND_PROG_LATENCY 185000 at ssd_config.h:95), and tR once per flash-page read (ssd.c:394-398). Only the channel transfer scales with bytes (ssd.c:403-405, 424). User programs are ONESHOT-sized (conv_ftl.c:951), and GLOBAL_WB_SIZE scales with ONESHOT (ssd_config.h:105). Program cycle per LUN is 223.9 / 262.8 / 340.6 us for 32K / 64K / 128K, so peak program bandwidth is 2233 -> 3805 -> 5871 MiB/s (1.7x and 2.6x). The write buffer becomes 1 -> 2 -> 4 MiB. GC time per 8 MiB line at 90% valid is about 17.4 / 10.9 / 7.7 ms of LUN time for <=32K / 64K / 128K.
all_claims.impact_on_results: MAP=64K/128K get a faster NAND and a larger buffer, both unrelated to mapping granularity. Their GC and throughput results will look better for reasons the paper would wrongly attribute to the mapping unit.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Keep per-byte NAND cost constant: for 64K/128K set NAND_PROG_LATENCY = 185000*FLASH_PAGE_SIZE/KB(32) (370 us / 740 us). Optionally scale NAND_READ_LATENCY_* the same way, which models a 64K unit as two 32K pages, and decide explicitly whether GLOBAL_WB_SIZE should stay at the formula value. At minimum, document this confound.

all_claims.title: GC onset lands at very different times inside the 60 s window, so the 60 s mean mixes pre-GC and GC phases differently per configuration
all_claims.evidence: GC fires only at credit exhaustion with free_line_cnt<=2 (conv_ftl.c:100-108, 815-822). Write credits = pgs_per_line, refilled with the victim's ipc (conv_ftl.c:154-161, 770). Onset therefore needs 380 user-written lines per partition (conv_ftl.c:168-182, 250-266, 349-350), which is 12,160 MiB of page-writes and does not depend on MAP (see the geometry above). For bs<=MAP at about 64K IOPS that is 48.6 / 24.3 / 12.2 / 6.1 / 3.0 / 1.5 s for MAP 4K..128K. For bs>=MAP it is 12,160 MiB / BW, and the window contains no GC at all if BW < 202.7 MiB/s. MAP=4K/bs=4K at the measured 250 MiB/s reaches GC at about 48.6 s, so roughly 11 s of GC are in the window; a run at 230 MiB/s would get only about 7 s.
all_claims.impact_on_results: Averages across configurations are not comparable phase-for-phase, and run-to-run throughput jitter changes how much GC is included (higher variance for MAP=4K/bs=4K). Pre-GC 4K numbers are emulator-CPU bound: NAND headroom is 2233 vs 250 MiB/s.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Add write_bw_log/write_iops_log/write_lat_log with log_avg_msec=1000 (plus per_job_logs) so the pre-GC and GC phases can be reported separately, and record the measured GC-onset second per run. Keep ramp_time=0 as requested.

all_claims.title: WA trajectory with fio's default randommap: a cliff at onset, then decay; the GC phase in the window is not steady state
all_claims.affects: All combos; shape differs between bs>=MAP and bs<MAP
all_claims.evidence: Victim selection is greedy minimum-vpc: the pqueue is a min-heap via victim_line_cmp_pri 'next > curr' (conv_ftl.c:68-71, pqueue.c:62-66). Foreground GC always forces (conv_ftl.c:656, 820). A faithful timing-free replay of this logic (scratchpad wasim.py, uniform permutation per pass) gives: for bs>=MAP the first pass has no overwrites, and right after onset WA is about 7-9 (MAP=4K/bs=4K: 8.8, 7.5, 7.3, 6.8 per 160K-write window), decaying to about 1.5 by the end of pass 2 and spiking again at pass 3 (both 16K/16K and 128K/128K show this). For bs<MAP, WA rises gradually after onset toward the 7.6-8.6 steady state (128K/4K reaches 7.6 after about 2.3 GiB; 32K/4K reaches 8.3 after about 6.9 GiB). Steady state with 7% OP and greedy GC is about 8.1-8.6 for every MAP. When bs<MAP, the physical cost per host byte is WA x MAP/bs (e.g. 7.6 x 32 = 244x at 128K/4K).
all_claims.impact_on_results: Post-onset numbers depend on where in this transient the 60 s window ends, which in turn depends on throughput. For MAP=4K/bs=4K the estimated NAND-limited rate after onset is about 50-55K IOPS (about 195-215 MiB/s), a dip of only ~15-20% over the last ~11 s, so the 60 s mean comes to roughly 240 MiB/s.
all_claims.suggested_fix: Report the time series (C5). If steady-state GC behaviour is needed, add a separate preconditioned run variant, but keep the requested fresh-device run as the primary one. State the fio randommap/randrepeat defaults in the report.

all_claims.title: GC mechanics confirmed: foreground only, one victim per trigger, copies at flash-page granularity, erase is free, runs inline in the dispatcher
all_claims.evidence: should_gc and should_gc_high both use threshold 2 (conv_ftl.c:16-24, 370-371). There is no background/idle GC; foreground_gc runs a single do_gc per credit exhaustion (conv_ftl.c:815-822) from conv_write on the dispatcher CPU (conv_ftl.c:1011-1012). do_gc walks flashpg x ch x lun (conv_ftl.c:773-807). clean_one_flashpg issues one NAND_READ with xfer = pgsz*cnt of the valid pages (conv_ftl.c:702-727), then gc_write_page per valid page; that is a NOP except on the last page of a oneshot, which issues one ONESHOT program (conv_ftl.c:617-631). Erase uses NAND_ERASE_LATENCY=0 (ssd_config.h:96, ssd.c:433-439). The copy unit is therefore one MAP page and the read unit is one flash page. Free-line exhaustion would hit a NULL dereference (conv_ftl.c:266-269), but it cannot happen here: the LPN space (358.85 lines per partition) is below the 380-line GC threshold, so victims always exist (no crash in any simulated combo). Inline GC CPU cost is small: about 2048 page checks per 8 MiB line, against one GC per ~ipc*4 host writes.
all_claims.impact_on_results: GC cost is LUN occupancy only, and erase is free (the default), so GC cost is somewhat underestimated in absolute terms. This applies equally to every MAP.
all_claims.suggested_fix: none (document as model properties)

all_claims.title: GC read-to-write dependency is not enforced and GC ops start at 'now'; GC programs to idle LUNs skip channel time
all_claims.evidence: clean_one_flashpg stores completed_time but never uses it (conv_ftl.c:699, 726). gc_write_page uses stime=0 (conv_ftl.c:621), so cmd_stime = __get_ioclock() (ssd.c:365) and a copy program can be scheduled before its source read finishes. For an idle LUN, chnl_stime = cmd_stime is slightly earlier than the cur_time chmodel reads later (channel_model.c:33), so chmodel returns request_time with zero transfer time (channel_model.c:64-68). lunp->gc_endtime is written but never read (conv_ftl.c:803).
all_claims.impact_on_results: GC latency is slightly underestimated (at most one 38.9-155.6 us channel transfer per idle-LUN program, plus missing read-to-write serialization). Small compared with the C1/C4 effects.
all_claims.suggested_fix: none required; mention in the limitations

all_claims.title: 4KB-specific constants are irrelevant for a write-only randwrite
all_claims.evidence: (a) ssd.c:394-398 'xfer_size == 4096' picks pg_4kb_rd_lat. It only applies to reads, and in randwrite the only reads are GC reads with xfer = pgsz*cnt (conv_ftl.c:722). That equals 4096 only for MAP=4K with exactly one valid page in the flash page, and the latency differs by 253 ns (35,760 vs 36,013 ns, ±6,000 LSB/MSB; ssd_config.h:89-93): <1%. (b) conv_ftl.c:867 fw_4kb_rd_lat is in conv_read only, so it is never executed. (c) The ssd.c:355 per-4KB term (460 ns * ceil(len/4K)) uses host bytes (conv_ftl.c:966) and is independent of MAP; it only sets the early-completion latency (5,612 ns at 4K). (d) ssd.c:269 fw_ch_xfer_lat is 0, and 128/4096 integer-divides to 0 anyway.
all_claims.impact_on_results: None on the MAP comparison for writes. The 'pg == 4KB' comments (ssd.c:73, ssd.h:65, 141) are only stale documentation.
all_claims.suggested_fix: none

all_claims.title: Host/NAND coupling for bs>=MAP works only through the shared write buffer, which blocks the whole device on one partition's GC
all_claims.evidence: With early completion the host never waits for NAND (conv_ftl.c:1015-1021). The only coupling is buffer_allocate failing (conv_ftl.c:961-963), which stops the dispatcher consuming the SQ (io.c:474-475, 523-527). The buffer and PCIe model are shared by all 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:397-405). GC NAND ops queue on the partition's 4 LUNs after already-scheduled user programs (ssd.c:422-429, 435-437), which delays buffer releases (io.c:668-673). With 1 MiB = 256 x 4K slots, a ~17 ms GC (MAP=4K, ~90% valid victim) in one partition fills the buffer with that partition's writes and stalls the host for the other three as well. Pending internal ops stay at or below WB/ONESHOT = 32, so C2 does not occur.
all_claims.impact_on_results: GC slowdown for bs>=MAP is modeled, and the head-of-line blocking is part of the model. The host sees it as SQ queueing inside fio clat, not as device-side latency.
all_claims.suggested_fix: none; describe this in the methodology

all_claims.title: rmmod+insmod resets FTL state but not the backing data
all_claims.evidence: conv_init_namespace rebuilds maptbl/rmap/lines/write pointers from scratch (conv_ftl.c:300-358, 386-395), so every run starts with 384 free lines. The reserved region is only memremap'ed and never cleared (main.c:446-447; no memset of storage in main.c). The data path is a flat logical image (io.c:107-111).
all_claims.impact_on_results: Timing is fully reset per run as intended, and the fresh-device premise holds. Data content from the previous run persists, which is irrelevant for write-only timing.
all_claims.suggested_fix: none; record in the procedure that the FTL resets on insmod but the data is not zeroed

verified.title: Write-buffer over-release when bs < MAP removes all NAND/GC back-pressure on the host
verified.affects: All 15 bs<MAP combos: MAP=8K bs=4K; 16K bs=4,8K; 32K bs=4,8,16K; 64K bs=4..32K; 128K bs=4..64K
verified.evidence: Allocation uses host bytes: conv_ftl.c:961 'buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba))'. Release uses full mapping units: every time a oneshot page completes, conv_ftl.c:1001-1008 calls 'schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz)', and that release happens at NAND completion (io.c:668-673). For aligned bs<MAP each host write is exactly 1 LPN, i.e. one MAP page (conv_ftl.c:937-938). So one oneshot page = pgs_per_oneshotpg writes allocating pgs_per_oneshotpg*bs bytes, but ONESHOT bytes are released. Net gain per oneshot is ONESHOT*(1-bs/MAP): +16K per 4 writes at MAP=8K/bs=4K, +124K per write at MAP=128K/bs=4K. buffer_release just adds with no clamp (ssd.c:39-46), and the only place the host is throttled is buffer_allocate returning 0 when remaining<size (ssd.c:29-31 -> conv_ftl.c:962-963 -> io.c:474-475, 525-526). Completion time itself is NAND-independent under WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1: ret->nsecs_target = nsecs_xfer_completed, i.e. the fw+PCIe time from ssd.c:349-360 (conv_ftl.c:965-967, 1015-1021). At 64K IOPS 'remaining' grows by roughly 0.25-7.6 GiB/s, so after the first few ms the buffer never blocks.
verified.impact_on_results: For bs<MAP the measured IOPS/BW reflects only the emulator's dispatcher CPU path. NAND program amplification (MAP bytes programmed per bs-byte write) and the whole GC cost are invisible to fio. MAP=128K/bs=4K would therefore show roughly the same ~64K IOPS as MAP=4K/bs=4K, even though NAND demand is 32x higher and GC starts at 1.5 s. With correct coupling, NAND capacity would be about 47K IOPS before GC and about 4.2K IOPS (~16 MiB/s) at the steady GC WA of 7.6. Any paper conclusion about small writes under coarse mapping drawn from these points would be wrong.
verified.suggested_fix: In the experiment copy, buffer whole mapping units so that allocation equals release: replace conv_ftl.c:961-963 with 'size_t wb = (end_lpn - start_lpn + 1) * spp->pgsz; allocated_buf_size = buffer_allocate(wbuf, wb); if (allocated_buf_size < wb) return false;'. This is unchanged for bs>=MAP (aligned) and satisfies the assert at ssd.c:23, since WB (1/2/4 MiB) >= MAP. Otherwise, drop bs<MAP from the matrix or report it as invalid.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the code at commit 61c90f7 and the core mechanism holds. The overstatements are in "all" and in the predicted symptom.

**Confirmed, line by line**
- **Allocation is in host bytes.** conv_ftl.c:961 calls `buffer_allocate(wbuf, LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba))`.
- **Release is in whole oneshot pages.** conv_ftl.c:1001-1008 calls `schedule_internal_operation(..., spp->pgs_per_oneshotpg * spp->pgsz)`, which is ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE. It is queued with target `nsecs_completed`, the NAND program end. The io worker calls `buffer_release` when that time arrives (io.c:668-673).
- **An aligned bs<MAP write is exactly one LPN.** See conv_ftl.c:937-938. There is no read-modify-write, so each such write programs a full MAP page.
- **The accounting gap matches the claim.** pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT/pgsz (ssd.c:100). Each oneshot therefore allocates pgs_per_oneshotpg×bs and releases ONESHOT. That is +16K per 4 writes at MAP=8K/bs=4K and +124K per write at MAP=128K/bs=4K.
- **Release is unclamped.** `buffer_release` just adds (ssd.c:39-46).
- **The buffer is the only throttle tied to NAND.** `buffer_allocate` returns 0 (ssd.c:29-31). conv_write then returns false (962-963), `__nvmev_proc_io` returns false and `nvmev_proc_io_sq` breaks.
- **Completion time ignores NAND.** With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 and no FUA, `nsecs_target` comes from `ssd_advance_write_buffer`, which is firmware time plus PCIe time (ssd.c:349-360).
- **GC never touches the buffer.** The only `buffer_allocate`/release site is conv_write. GC NAND time affects the host only by pushing `lun->next_lun_avail_time`, and through that the release times.
- **Suggested fix is sound.** Allocating `(end_lpn-start_lpn+1)*pgsz` balances allocate and release for bs<MAP. Nothing changes for aligned bs≥MAP. GLOBAL_WB_SIZE is 32×ONESHOT, which is ≥ MAP, so the assert at ssd.c:23 holds.

**Partly wrong**
1. **"Removes all back-pressure" is too strong.** Releases are NAND-paced, so `remaining` cannot grow faster than NAND user bandwidth minus allocation. It does not grow at the 0.25-7.6 GiB/s host-side figure. The buffer still binds whenever host bs-bytes/s exceeds NAND user bandwidth B_u. The host is then throttled at B_u/bs instead of B_u/MAP, i.e. MAP/bs times too loose, not unthrottled.
   - Example, MAP=128K/bs=64K: PCIe caps the host near 3.3 GB/s. Pre-GC NAND is about 16 LUNs × 128K / (164 µs xfer + 185 µs program), roughly 6 GB/s. After GC starts (about 2 s), B_u ≈ 6/WA falls below 3.3 GB/s once WA > 1.8, so the buffer binds at 2× the correct rate.
   - Back-pressure is effectively gone only for large MAP/bs ratios. MAP=128K/bs=4K is one such case: NAND is about 45.8K oneshots/s against 64K IOPS demand.
2. **The predicted ~64K IOPS at MAP=128K/bs=4K, set purely by the dispatcher, does not follow from the code.** Nothing bounds the NAND backlog, so one pending release item per oneshot piles up with far-future targets. They all go into a single io worker's queue, because CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ is defined in nvmev.h:12, fio uses one SQ, and the queue holds NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO=16384 entries.
   - **Dispatcher slows down.** `__insert_req_sorted` (io.c:263-272) walks back from the tail past every pending future item for each near-now host completion, so it is O(P) per I/O on the dispatcher.
   - **Worker slows down.** The worker loop scans every entry on each pass (io.c:621-694, no break).
   - **I/Os can be lost.** Near capacity, `__allocate_work_queue_entry` returns NULL (io.c:301-304). The release is then silently dropped (io.c:365-367), and so is the host completion (io.c:325-327), even though its SQ entry was already consumed. That can hang fio until the NVMe timeout.
   - **Channel timing stops being modelled.** Once LUN drift passes NR_CREDIT_ENTRIES×4 µs ≈ 393 ms, `chmodel_request` returns `request_time` with no transfer time and prints an unratelimited NVMEV_ERROR on every request (channel_model.c:66-71).

So bs<MAP results would be dominated by these artifacts or fail outright. They would not be a clean dispatcher-only number. This makes the blocker worse, not weaker.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The blocker stands. For bs<MAP (aligned), conv_write allocates bs bytes from the write buffer (conv_ftl.c:961). Each completed oneshot page releases the full ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE (conv_ftl.c:1007), and that release only happens at NAND completion (io.c:671). The net over-release per oneshot is ONESHOT×(1−bs/MAP), with no clamp (ssd.c:39-46). Because WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 makes completion time independent of NAND, the write buffer is the only coupling between NAND/GC and the host.

The bug loosens that coupling by a factor of MAP/bs rather than removing it entirely. The host can sustain NAND user bandwidth divided by bs instead of divided by MAP. For ratio-2 pairs after GC starts (e.g. MAP=128K/bs=64K, MAP=8K/bs=4K), the buffer can still throttle, just 2× too loosely. For large ratios such as MAP=128K/bs=4K it effectively never throttles.

The NAND backlog has no bound, so pending release work items pile up in one io worker queue capped at 16384 entries. Each host completion's sorted insert costs O(n) (io.c:263-272), and the worker scans the whole queue on every pass. When the queue is nearly full, both releases and host completions are silently dropped (io.c:301-304, 325-327, 365-367), which can lose I/Os. Once drift exceeds about 393 ms, the channel model stops charging transfer time and logs an error on every request (channel_model.c:66-71).

Measured bs<MAP points would therefore be invalid, either inflated or distorted by emulator artifacts, or the run could hang. They would not simply show ~64K IOPS. The fix is valid: allocate (end_lpn−start_lpn+1)×pgsz at conv_ftl.c:961-963 and fail if less is granted. It leaves bs≥MAP unchanged and passes the ssd.c:23 assert. The other option is to drop the 15 bs<MAP combinations or mark them invalid.

verdicts.reasoning:
The code confirms the core bug.
- conv_ftl.c:961-963 allocates LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba), the host bytes.
- conv_ftl.c:1001-1008 schedules a release of pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz each time last_pg_in_wordline() is true.
- io.c:668-673 performs that release when the NAND completion time is reached.
- buffer_release (ssd.c:39-46) only adds, with no clamp. buffer_refill is used only by ZNS.
- For aligned bs<MAP, start_lpn equals end_lpn (conv_ftl.c:937-938), so each write is one LPN.
- Under WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1, completion is nsecs_xfer_completed: fw_wbuf_lat0 + lat1 + PCIe (ssd.c:349-360, conv_ftl.c:1015-1021).

Worked examples:
- MAP=16K, bs=4K: pgsz=16K, FLASH=ONESHOT=32K, pgs_per_oneshotpg=2. Two writes allocate 8K, and the oneshot releases 32K, so the net is +24K. This matches ONESHOT*(1-bs/MAP).
- MAP=128K, bs=4K: pgs_per_oneshotpg=1, so each write allocates 4K and releases 128K, a net of +124K.
- The write buffer is shared across the 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:398-405). GLOBAL_WB_SIZE is 1, 2 or 4 MiB.
- My NAND figure for MAP=128K before GC is about 46-47K writes/s: per channel, 2 LUNs x (164us transfer + 185us program), across 8 channels. This agrees with the claim.

Where the claim is wrong or overstated:

(1) Back-pressure is not removed in principle. Releases occur at the NAND completion rate S, so remaining changes by S*ONESHOT - h*bs. The host is still capped at (MAP/bs) times the NAND user-write rate. The 0.25-7.6 GiB/s growth figures hold only while NAND keeps up. In practice the cap is far above CPU speed when MAP/bs >= 4. A large surplus also builds before GC, so the buffer effectively never blocks within 60 s for most combos. For bs=MAP/2 in steady-state GC, the cap (about 2x the NAND user rate) can be lower than the host rate, so throttling can return once the surplus is used up.

(2) The predicted symptom ("MAP=128K/bs=4K shows about 64K IOPS, the same as MAP=4K, reflecting only the dispatcher CPU path") is not supported. With the buffer decoupled, the backlog of pending internal release ops grows without bound whenever the host outruns NAND. For MAP=128K/bs=4K this happens even before GC (46K/s vs 64K/s or more), and in every bs<MAP case once GC starts. This has three effects:
- (a) __insert_req_sorted (io.c:264-274) walks backward from the tail past every pending future-target internal op for each host op. The io worker loop (io.c:621-) also scans the whole list each pass. Dispatcher cost per IO therefore grows with the backlog, which creates an unintended coupling to NAND backlog. Measured IOPS would follow emulator list-walk overhead, not a CPU path that stays the same for every MAP.
- (b) NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO is 16384 per worker (nvmev.h:58). With CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ, one SQ maps to one worker. Once that is exceeded, __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-304). schedule_internal_operation then silently drops the release (io.c:365-366), and __enqueue_io_req silently drops the host command (io.c:325-327). That command never gets a CQ entry, so fio can stall or hit nvme timeouts. "IO queue is almost full" appears in dmesg.
- (c) The 64K IOPS measured at MAP=4K was taken with proper coupling and may itself be limited by NAND or GC, so it does not establish a CPU-only rate.

The blocker verdict and the suggested fix are correct. Allocating (end_lpn-start_lpn+1)*pgsz is unchanged for aligned bs>=MAP. Its largest allocation is 128K, which is below WB, so the assert at ssd.c:23 holds. It bounds the pending internal ops to about WB/ONESHOT = 32.

verified.impact_on_results: Expected outcomes are hung I/O and nvme timeouts/resets, or IOPS collapses caused by emulator list-walk and printk overhead rather than by the SSD model. Either way the run is invalid.
verified.suggested_fix: Fix C1. After every run, also save dmesg and grep for 'IO queue is almost full', 'Need to increase array size', 'No free entry' and 'nvme.*timeout'. Discard any run that shows them.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the code in upstream_tmp (61c90f7). Almost all of the mechanism is correct; two details are wrong.

Confirmed in the code:
- Write path (conv_ftl.c:961-1009): conv_write allocates LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba) from wbuf. Every time last_pg_in_wordline is true it calls schedule_internal_operation(..., pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz), so it releases a full ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE at NAND completion time.

  - With WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1, the CQE target is the write-buffer/PCIe time (conv_ftl.c:1015-1021), so iodepth does not bound the NAND backlog either.

- Worker pool: cpus=3,4,5 gives dispatcher=3 and nr_io_workers=2 (main.c:509-520). Workers are chosen round-robin (io.c:25-31, BY_SQ is not defined in Kbuild), each with NR_MAX_PARALLEL_IO=16384 entries (nvmev.h:58).

That command never gets a data copy or a CQE.
- O(pending) cost:
  - __insert_req_sorted walks back from the tail over every entry whose target is later than both the new target and latest_nsecs (io.c:264-274). A host entry with a near-now target therefore walks over every far-future internal entry.
  - The worker loop visits every list entry on each pass, with no early break (io.c:624-695).
- Channel horizon:
  - NR_CREDIT_ENTRIES=98304 and UNIT_TIME_INTERVAL=4000 ns, giving 393 ms.

  - NVMEV_ERROR is a plain printk(KERN_ERR) (nvmev.h:41).
- Numbers:
  - xfer_lat is 152 ns per 128 B, so a 128K transfer takes 155.6 us. With tPROG 185 us that is 340.6 us per LUN, or about 2936 programs/s per LUN and about 47K/s over 16 LUNs. This matches the 46,969/s figure.
  - With 64K/s demand, the backlog grows about 0.36 s per second and reaches the horizon after about 1.1 s.
  - At the horizon, the average cost per op is about 250 us, so pending entries are about 393 ms / 250 us x 16, roughly 25K. This matches the claim.

Wrong or inaccurate:
1. The constants are at channel_model.h:7-8, not 127-128. This is minor.
2. The suggested dmesg check is wrong for queue exhaustion. The code is WARN_ON_ONCE("IO queue is almost full"), and on this kernel (6.8.0-142, asm-generic/bug.h:110-116) WARN_ON_ONCE(cond) only evaluates !!cond. It never prints the string. dmesg shows only a generic "WARNING: CPU: N PID: M at .../io.c:302 __allocate_work_queue_entry+..." with a stack trace, once per module load. Grepping for 'IO queue is almost full' will never match, so the proposed discard filter would miss exactly the failure that drops CQEs.

This can throttle host submission down to NAND capacity before the 32K-entry pool is exhausted. The more likely symptom is then an emulator-bound IOPS collapse rather than hangs. The claim already hedges with "either way the run is invalid", so the conclusion stands.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The core finding is confirmed by the code. For bs<MAP, conv_write allocates bs bytes from the write buffer but releases a full ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE per programmed oneshot. The buffer therefore inflates and no longer throttles. Early completion means iodepth does not bound NAND work either, so the NAND backlog and the number of pending internal buffer-release entries are unbounded.

That backlog has these consequences:
- Each of the 2 workers (cpus=3,4,5) has 16384 entries. When a worker's free list runs out, __enqueue_io_req returns silently after the SQ entry was already consumed, so that command never gets a data copy or a CQE. The expected result is I/O hang, nvme timeout and reset.
- Sorted insertion (io.c:264-274) and the worker loop (io.c:624-695) both cost O(pending).
- When a LUN's backlog exceeds 98,304 x 4 us = 393 ms (channel_model.h:7-8, not 127-128), every further NAND op prints an unratelimited KERN_ERR "Need to increase array size" and skips channel transfer time.

The estimates are consistent with the model: about 47K programs/s capacity for MAP=128K, the horizon reached after about 1.1 s at 64K/s demand, and about 25K pending entries at the horizon. However, the dispatcher's O(pending) insert may itself throttle host IOPS before the pool is exhausted, so the symptom may be emulator-bound IOPS collapse rather than hangs. Either way the bs<MAP runs are invalid.

Correction to the detection step: WARN_ON_ONCE("IO queue is almost full") does not print its string. Grep dmesg for 'WARNING:.*__allocate_work_queue_entry' (or 'io.c:302'), 'Need to increase array size', 'No free entry', 'nvme.*(timeout|reset|abort)', and the kernel taint flag 'W'. Do not grep for 'IO queue is almost full'.

verdicts.reasoning:
The mechanism is in the code, but the capacity figure, the timeline estimates and the suggested dmesg grep are wrong. I checked the code and also the base runs already recorded on this server (exp/results).

Code paths that hold:
- conv_write (conv_ftl.c:961-1008) reserves bs bytes of write buffer per command. Each oneshot program calls schedule_internal_operation(req->sq_id, nsecs_completed, wbuf, pgs_per_oneshotpg*pgsz), which gives back a full oneshot (32K, or MAP when MAP>=64K). buffer_release (ssd.c:39-47) has no upper limit. So when bs<MAP the buffer never fills, nothing pushes back on the host, and lun->next_lun_avail_time can run ahead of real time.
- When the free list runs out, __allocate_work_queue_entry returns NULL (io.c:301-304). __enqueue_io_req then returns without doing anything (io.c:326). __nvmev_proc_io still returns true, so nvmev_proc_io_sq moves past the SQ entry (io.c:523-533) and that command never gets a CQE.
- __insert_req_sorted walks back from the tail over every entry whose target is in the future (io.c:266-274). The worker loop visits every entry on every pass and calls local_clock() for each one (io.c:624-695). Both are O(pending).
- channel_model.c:73-76: when request_time_offs >= NR_CREDIT_ENTRIES (98,304 x 4 us = 393 ms) it calls NVMEV_ERROR, which is a plain printk(KERN_ERR) (nvmev.h:41), and returns request_time, i.e. zero transfer time. A "No free entry" printk also exists.
- MAP=128K numbers: xfer_lat is 152 ns per 128 B, so a 128K transfer takes 155.6 us. Add tPROG 185 us for 340.6 us per LUN; 16 LUNs give about 46.98K programs/s. The claimed ~46,969/s is correct.

1. Usable work-queue capacity is one worker, not "~32.7K total". CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ is defined (nvmev.h:12), so the worker is (sqid-1)%nr_io_workers (io.c:25-28). Internal ops are queued with req->sq_id, so they land on the same worker as the host command. With numjobs=1 all observed traffic was on QID 1. The limit is therefore one worker's 16,384 entries (about 16,383 usable), and "25K pending out of 32.7K" cannot happen.
2. The MAP=128K/bs=4K timeline does not match what ran here. In the 10 s base smoke run (exp/results/pre_smoke_test/base/map128k_bs4k_r1), IOPS in 0.5 s bins were 56.2K, then 46.8K, 46.8K and 47.2K. That is the NAND limit, not 64K. The O(pending) insertion walk is consistent with acting as a brake that holds the host at that rate. GC started at 2.2 s, not 1.5 s. The first 'Need to increase array size' line appeared at 2.66 s, after GC started, so the 393 ms limit was not reached about 1 s into the run before GC. That run had no io.c:302 WARNING and no nvme timeout. It did print 1,859,673 chmodel lines in 10 s, and IOPS then dropped to about 23-35K.
3. The predicted overflows for MAP=32K/bs=4K (7-10 s) and 16K/bs=4K (20-25 s) did not happen in the 60 s base runs. Results:
   - 32k/4k: 23.7K IOPS, 8.23M chmodel lines.
   - 16k/4k: 43.0K IOPS, 6.76M chmodel lines.
   - 8k/4k: 68.2K IOPS, 8.24M chmodel lines, plus one "No free entry" line.
   All three ended with fio_exit 0, maximum clat 7.6 ms or less, and no io.c:302 WARNING and no nvme timeout.
   The overflow did happen for map32k_bs16k_r1:
   - +24.97 s: WARNING at io.c:302
   - +55 s: QID 1 nvme timeouts
   - +85 s: controller reset
   - +147 s: controller disabled, then EIO; fio exited with code 1.
4. The suggested grep would miss the event. The code is WARN_ON_ONCE("IO queue is almost full"), which uses the string as the condition. The kernel prints "WARNING: CPU: 3 ... at .../io.c:302 __allocate_work_queue_entry+...", only once per module load, and never the text 'IO queue is almost full'. That run's kernel.log has 0 matches for "almost full".
5. Minor points:
   - The constants are at channel_model.h:7-8; the file has only 46 lines, so the cited lines 127-128 do not exist.
   - The internal entry is queued when conv_write schedules the program (in the dispatcher), not when the oneshot completes.
   - If allocating an internal op fails, that buffer release is silently lost.
   - The SQ index moves forward after the enqueue fails (the FTL state is already updated), not before.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
With bs<MAP, the base write path (buffer reserved = bs, released = oneshot size, no cap) removes the write-buffer backpressure. The NAND backlog can then grow, and the emulator has these failure paths:
- One internal entry is queued per oneshot program, with its target at the future NAND completion time.
- Insertion and the worker loop both cost O(pending).
- Beyond the 393 ms channel-model window, chmodel_request prints an unratelimited KERN_ERR line ('Need to increase array size', also 'No free entry') and charges zero transfer time.
- When the free list runs out, an NVMe command is consumed without a CQE, which leads to nvme timeout, reset and controller disable.

The capacity is one worker's 16,384 entries, not about 32.7K. Under CONFIG_NVMEV_IO_WORKER_BY_SQ, all traffic from the single fio job (QID 1) and its internal ops goes to one worker.

The O(pending) insertion walk is consistent with acting as an accidental brake. Before GC, MAP=128K/bs=4K ran at the NAND limit (about 47K IOPS, measured), so the 393 ms window was first exceeded only after GC began. In practice, every bs<MAP combination run so far produced millions of chmodel printk lines: 8k/4k 8.2M, 16k/4k 6.8M, 32k/4k 8.2M, 128k/4k 1.86M in 10 s. Those results are therefore unreliable, because zero transfer time and printk load mix into the measurement.

The work queue overflowed only in map32k_bs16k (WARNING at +25 s, nvme timeouts at +55 s, reset at +85 s, device disabled with EIO at +147 s). The 32k/4k and 16k/4k runs did not overflow within 60 s, contrary to the 7-10 s and 20-25 s estimates.

For run screening, grep dmesg for 'io.c:302|__allocate_work_queue_entry|WARNING:', not 'IO queue is almost full', which never appears. Keep the 'Need to increase array size', 'No free entry' and 'nvme.*(timeout|reset)' patterns.

verified.title: Partial writes (bs<MAP): no read-modify-write read is modeled; data integrity is preserved by the flat logical backing store
verified.affects: All bs<MAP combos (the performance model only)
verified.evidence: conv_write issues only invalidate + allocate + program (conv_ftl.c:971-1013). The old MAP page is marked invalid wholesale (conv_ftl.c:980-985) and no NAND_READ of the old ppa is ever issued. The program does charge a full MAP unit per write: swr.xfer_size = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg (conv_ftl.c:951) and every lpn consumes one pgsz page. Data is never handled by the FTL: there is no memcpy in conv_ftl.c or ssd.c (grep), gc_write_page says 'move valid page data (already in DRAM)' (conv_ftl.c:597), and the io worker copies to ns->mapped + (slba<<LBA_BITS) (io.c:39-42, 107-111) or to the DMA target storage_start+offset (io.c:236). The bytes in the rest of the mapping unit therefore stay intact and readable.
verified.impact_on_results: No data is silently dropped. Timing still underestimates the cost of a partial write: the RMW read (one tR of about 36 us plus a MAP-sized channel transfer, e.g. 38.9 us at 32K) is missing for every bs<MAP write to an already mapped LPN. Program-side amplification (MAP/bs) is modeled, but only becomes visible once C1 is fixed.
verified.suggested_fix: Optional: in conv_write, if (nr_lba*512 < pgsz) and the old ppa is mapped, issue a NAND_READ of the old ppa (xfer=pgsz) before the program and set the program stime to at least that read's completion. Otherwise state in the paper that the RMW read is not modeled.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced the code at upstream 61c90f7 and it supports every part of the claim.

1. The write path does no read-modify-write. In conv_write (conv_ftl.c:925-1023), each LPN in [start_lpn, end_lpn] goes through the same steps: get_maptbl_ent, then mark_page_invalid + set_rmap_ent(INVALID_LPN) if the page is mapped (lines 980-985), then get_new_page / set_maptbl_ent / set_rmap_ent / mark_page_valid / advance_write_pointer. The only NAND command it builds is swr with .cmd = NAND_WRITE (lines 947-952). That command is issued only when last_pg_in_wordline is true (line 1001 onward). No NAND_READ is built anywhere in conv_write. A sub-MAP write (bs < MAP) gives start_lpn == end_lpn, so the old pgsz page is invalidated whole and its content is never read.

2. Each write is charged a full MAP slot. ssd_init_params sets pgsz = secsz * secs_per_pg, which equals MAP after the planned change at ssd.c:73. pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE/pgsz, and swr.xfer_size = pgsz * pgs_per_oneshotpg (line 951). So every LPN, including one written by a 4K I/O when MAP=32K, uses one pgsz slot in the write pointer. Programs are batched per oneshot page, so one program is charged per pgs_per_oneshotpg LPNs. In terms of NAND space and program bandwidth, the MAP/bs amplification is modeled.

3. The FTL never touches the data. grep finds no memcpy or memset in conv_ftl.c or ssd.c. gc_write_page (conv_ftl.c:597) only remaps metadata. The data copy happens in io.c __do_perform_io: memcpy into nvmev_vdev->ns[nsid].mapped + (slba << LBA_BITS) for writes, and the reverse for reads. In the DMA path, ioat_dma_submit goes to storage_start + offset. ns->mapped is set from the flat memremap of storage_start (main.c:446, conv_ftl.c:412). Storage is therefore indexed by logical byte offset and is independent of the PPA mapping. A partial write changes only its own bytes, and the rest of the MAP unit stays intact and readable. No data is silently lost.

4. The impact numbers are right. A NAND_READ with xfer_size != 4096 uses pg_rd_lat = 36013 ± 6000 ns (30.0 us LSB / 42.0 us MSB, average about 36 us). The channel model uses xfer_lat = 128e9 / (800 * 2^20), which is 152 ns per 128 B. A 32K transfer is 256 units * 152 ns = 38.9 us, sent in 16K chunks because MAX_CH_XFER_SIZE is 16K. This matches the claim.

One nuance that does not refute the claim: WRITE_EARLY_COMPLETION=1 in the 970PRO bundle, so a write completes at the write-buffer time (nsecs_xfer_completed). A missing RMW read would therefore show up only indirectly, through LUN/channel occupancy, the write-buffer release time (schedule_internal_operation) and the write credit / GC pressure, not in the latency of each write. The claim correctly limits itself to saying the timing underestimates the cost.

I checked this against commit 61c90f7 using one case: MAP=32K, bs=4K, and a write at slba=8 (byte offset 4096) to an LPN that is already mapped.

Every cited line number matches the source. Minor nuance, not a refutation: the read is only actually needed when the old LPN is mapped. The claim already limits itself to "already mapped" LPNs, and the suggested fix includes that check.

For any write with bs < MAP to an already-mapped LPN, conv_write marks the old MAP-sized page invalid and programs a new MAP-sized page (xfer = pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg). verified.title: FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=MAP for 64K/128K changes the simulated NAND hardware and confounds the MAP comparison
verified.affects: MAP=64K and MAP=128K (all bs) compared against MAP<=32K
verified.evidence: tPROG is charged once per program regardless of size (ssd.c:427-428, NAND_PROG_LATENCY 185000 at ssd_config.h:95), and tR once per flash-page read (ssd.c:394-398). Only the channel transfer scales with bytes (ssd.c:403-405, 424). User programs are ONESHOT-sized (conv_ftl.c:951), and GLOBAL_WB_SIZE scales with ONESHOT (ssd_config.h:105). Program cycle per LUN is 223.9 / 262.8 / 340.6 us for 32K / 64K / 128K, so peak program bandwidth is 2233 -> 3805 -> 5871 MiB/s (1.7x and 2.6x). The write buffer becomes 1 -> 2 -> 4 MiB. GC time per 8 MiB line at 90% valid is about 17.4 / 10.9 / 7.7 ms of LUN time for <=32K / 64K / 128K.
verified.impact_on_results: MAP=64K/128K get a faster NAND and a larger buffer, both unrelated to mapping granularity. Their GC and throughput results will look better for reasons the paper would wrongly attribute to the mapping unit.
verified.suggested_fix: Keep per-byte NAND cost constant: for 64K/128K set NAND_PROG_LATENCY = 185000*FLASH_PAGE_SIZE/KB(32) (370 us / 740 us). Optionally scale NAND_READ_LATENCY_* the same way, which models a 64K unit as two 32K pages, and decide explicitly whether GLOBAL_WB_SIZE should stay at the formula value. At minimum, document this confound.

verdicts.reasoning:
I traced each part of the claim through commit 61c90f7 and it holds.

(1) Program cost does not depend on size. In ssd_advance_nand NAND_WRITE (ssd.c:420-431), one chmodel_request covers the whole ncmd->xfer_size (ssd.c:424). After that, a fixed spp->pg_wr_lat (= NAND_PROG_LATENCY 185000, set at ssd.c:117) is added once (ssd.c:428).

(2) Read sensing time is charged once per command. pg_rd_lat (or pg_4kb_rd_lat when xfer_size==4096) is added once (ssd.c:394-398). Only the channel transfer loop scales with bytes (ssd.c:403-415). GC reads are issued once per flash page by clean_one_flashpg (conv_ftl.c:717-727). do_gc iterates over flashpgs_per_blk (conv_ftl.c:773).

(3) Program size scales with the page. User programs are pgsz*pgs_per_oneshotpg = ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE (conv_ftl.c:951) and GC programs are the same (conv_ftl.c:627). So when FLASH_PAGE_SIZE=ONESHOT=64K or 128K, every tPROG covers 2x or 4x the bytes. For MAP<=32K the program is always 32K, so the per-byte NAND cost is constant across 4K..32K.

(4) The write buffer scales too. GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*ONESHOT*2 (ssd_config.h:105). It is passed to buffer_init (ssd.c:130, 314) and shared by all 4 partitions (conv_ftl.c:404). That gives 1, 2 and 4 MiB.

(5) The arithmetic is correct. Integer BANDWIDTH_TO_TX_TIME(800) = 152 ns per 128 B. That gives cycles of 223.9, 262.8 and 340.6 us. With 16 LUNs (4 partitions x 2 ch x 2 LUN), peak program bandwidth is 2233, 3805 and 5871 MiB/s. GC per LUN on a 2 MiB block at 90% valid comes to 17.45, 10.96 and 7.72 ms. I recomputed all of these. No other code path uses FLASH_PAGE_SIZE or pg_wr_lat to rescale latency (checked with grep). get_cell only alternates LSB/MSB per flash page.

So making FLASH_PAGE_SIZE equal to MAP for 64K and 128K does make the simulated NAND faster per byte and the buffer larger, independent of the mapping unit.

Three refinements, none of which overturns the claim:

(a) The 3805 and 5871 MiB/s figures are NAND-internal. Host writes are also charged to the shared PCIe model in ssd_advance_write_buffer (ssd.c:357, PCIE_BANDWIDTH 3360). That model caps host-visible throughput at about 3357 MiB/s (110 credits x 128 B per 4 us). So the pre-GC host ceiling goes from about 2233 to about 3.3 GiB/s for both 64K and 128K. The full 1.7x and 2.6x NAND advantage shows up in GC and steady-state LUN time, and in any case that is NAND-bound.

(b) The buffer-size difference only matters when bs >= MAP. When bs < MAP, conv_write allocates LBA_TO_BYTE(nr_lba) (conv_ftl.c:961). But every page-completing write releases a full ONESHOT (conv_ftl.c:1007-1008). The buffer's remaining count then inflates and stops throttling, for every MAP > bs (including 8K-32K). This is a separate artifact.

(c) The user explicitly asked for FLASH_PAGE_SIZE = MAP for 64K/128K and default values otherwise. Changing NAND_PROG_LATENCY therefore needs the user's decision. At minimum the confound must be documented.

It also doubles or quadruples GLOBAL_WB_SIZE to 2 or 4 MiB (ssd_config.h:105).

- NAND-internal peak program bandwidth: 2233 / 3805 / 5871 MiB/s

2) The channel cost per byte is fixed. xfer_lat = 128*1e9/MB(800) = 152 ns per 128 B (channel_model.h, nvmev.h MB=<<20). So 32K = 256 units = 38.9 us, 64K = 77.8 us and 128K = 155.6 us. The LUN cycle is therefore 223.9, 262.8 and 340.6 us. There are 16 LUNs (8 ch x 2 LUN, split into 4 partitions of 2ch x 2LUN). Peak program bandwidth is 16*32KiB/223.9us = 2233 MiB/s, 16*64KiB/262.8us = 3805 MiB/s and 16*128KiB/340.6us = 5871 MiB/s, which matches the claim. The channel does not cap this even at 128K: two LUNs need 2x155.6 = 311 us per channel, which is under 340.6 us.

3) Reads are charged one tR per flash page. GC's clean_one_flashpg issues a single NAND_READ for all valid pages of a flash page (xfer_size = pgsz*cnt, conv_ftl.c:717-726), and ssd.c:394-398 charges one tR (about 36 us) per command. User reads are also merged per flash page (conv_ftl.c:894-897).

4) The write buffer scales with ONESHOT. GLOBAL_WB_SIZE = 8*2*ONESHOT*2 (ssd_config.h:105), which gives 1, 2 and 4 MiB. It is shared by all partitions (conv_ftl.c:397-405) and released per wordline when the program completes (conv_ftl.c:1007).

5) GC example. Storage is 12G - 1MiB, so each partition is about 3 GiB. With BLKS_PER_PLN=384, blk_size = DIV_ROUND_UP(3GiB-256KiB, 384*4), which is about 2 MiB (64/32/16 oneshot pages). A line is 4 blocks = 8 MiB. At 90% valid, each LUN block has 1.8 MiB to move:
- 32K: 64 reads x (36 + 0.9x38.9 = 71 us) = 4.5 ms, plus 57.6 programs x 223.9 us = 12.9 ms, total 17.4 ms.
- 64K: 32 x 106 us = 3.4 ms, plus 28.8 x 262.8 us = 7.6 ms, total 10.9 ms.
- 128K: 16 x 176 us = 2.8 ms, plus 14.4 x 340.6 us = 4.9 ms, total 7.7 ms.
All three match the claim.

6) The NAND model really differs between the groups. For MAP<=32K the simulated NAND is the same in every case (32K page and oneshot). For MAP=64K/128K it is a different, faster per byte NAND with a larger buffer in bytes. MAP is therefore confounded with NAND throughput and GC cost. One check needs no simulation: the MAP=4K/bs=4K baseline of about 250 MiB/s is far below even the 2233 MiB/s peak.

Minor caveats, none of which refute the claim:
(a) The buffer formula keeps 2 oneshot pages per LUN in every case. The larger buffer in bytes is therefore a direct consequence of the larger oneshot, and it would stay proportionate if tPROG were scaled.
(b) The effect will be partly masked in some runs. Small-bs runs before GC appear to be CPU/IOPS-bound (about 64K IOPS measured). Large-bs runs at MAP>=64K are capped by PCIE_BANDWIDTH 3360 MB/s (about 3204 MiB/s) rather than by NAND, so the full 1.7x/2.6x gap will not show everywhere. The confound will show most strongly once GC starts.
(c) The fix needs a small addition. Scaling only tPROG leaves tR per byte lower for 64K/128K GC reads (one tR per 128K instead of four). Read latency should be scaled too, or the difference documented. Another fix the auditor did not mention also removes the confound: use one FLASH_PAGE_SIZE/ONESHOT (e.g. 128K) for all six MAP values, so that only MAP changes. The cost is that the baseline moves away from the stock 970PRO 32K page.
verdicts.corrected_statement:
The claim is right. For MAP=64K/128K, setting FLASH_PAGE_SIZE (and so ONESHOT_PAGE_SIZE) to MAP keeps the flat NAND_PROG_LATENCY of 185 us per program (ssd.c:428) and the single tR per flash-page read (ssd.c:394-398). Only the channel transfer grows with size (152 ns per 128 B). As a result:
- The LUN program cycle is 223.9 / 262.8 / 340.6 us for 32K / 64K / 128K.
- Peak NAND program bandwidth is 2233 / 3805 / 5871 MiB/s.
- GLOBAL_WB_SIZE is 1 / 2 / 4 MiB, always 2 oneshot pages per LUN.
- GC of an 8 MiB line at 90% valid takes about 17.4 / 10.9 / 7.7 ms per LUN.

So MAP>=64K runs on a faster per byte NAND model than MAP<=32K, which is a confound in the comparison.

Where the effect shows: pre-GC small-bs runs appear to be CPU/IOPS-bound, and large-bs runs at 64K/128K are capped by the PCIe model (3360 MB/s). The confound will show most strongly once GC starts.

Fixes:
- Scale NAND_PROG_LATENCY by FLASH_PAGE_SIZE/32K, i.e. 370 us for 64K and 740 us for 128K.
- Scale NAND_READ_LATENCY_* the same way so GC reads are not cheaper per byte, or document that they are.
- Alternatively, use the same FLASH_PAGE_SIZE (e.g. 128K) for all MAP values so only the mapping unit changes.

At minimum, the paper must document this confound.

The height of the cliff is understated. Re-running the auditor's own wasim.py at finer resolution, MAP=4K/bs=4K has WA of about 12-12.7 for roughly the first 300 MiB of host writes after onset. It falls to about 9 by +650 MiB and about 7.5 by +900 MiB. The 8.8/7.5/7.3/6.8 series starts about 340 MiB after onset, and the window that contains onset is mixed with writes from before onset. 16K/16K behaves the same way (about 11.5 at onset). Only 128K/128K starts at about 8.

Impact for 4K/4K, from my estimated NAND model: throughput right after onset is limited to about 34-36K IOPS (about 135-140 MiB/s), a dip of about 45% from 64K that lasts about 2-3 s. It then recovers to about 58-62K IOPS. The average after onset is about 52-53K IOPS, and the 60 s mean is still about 240 MiB/s. The per-second time series will therefore show a sharp, short drop, not a shallow 15-20% dip. The suggested fixes still apply: report the time series, state fio's randommap/randrepeat defaults, and use an optional preconditioned variant.
